articles.title: How Can Anything Beat n log n?
articles.body:
How Can Anything Beat n log n?
Section: Home / Post
Categories: Computer Science,
Tags: Algorithms, Entropy, Information Theory,
Recently, headlines have kept making the rounds about sub-$n \log n$ algorithms—first Duan et al. breaking Dijkstra’s $O(m + n \log n)$ sorting barrier for directed shortest paths, and then a preprint claiming sub-$n \log n$ integer multiplication.
My first reaction was skepticism. If a problem cares about ordering $n$ items, don’t you need $\log n$ steps to uniquely place each item, repeated $n$ times? That gives $n \log n$. How could you possibly do better?
The short answer is that $n \log n$ is not a universal speed limit. It is the lower bound of a specific model of computation. To see how algorithms beat it, we need to look at what $n \log n$ actually measures—and which assumptions those algorithms drop.
What $n \log n$ Actually Looks Like
Think of sorting $n$ items as routing each item down a decision tree into its final slot.
If you are only allowed to take 2-way comparison steps (< or >), every fork in the tree has 2 branches. Each step cuts the remaining slots in half. To route one item to its unique leaf among $n$ slots, it has to travel down roughly $\log_2 n$ levels.
Send all $n$ items down a tree of depth $\log_2 n$, and you pay $n \log_2 n$ total steps.
The Hidden Assumptions
That intuition feels airtight: if characterizing or placing a single item among $n$ slots takes $\log_2 n$ steps, and there are $n$ items to process, then any task requiring ordering or classification across $n$ items seems forced to pay $n \log_2 n$. Under two specific conditions, that reasoning is airtight:
- Black-box items: You cannot peek inside an item. Your only tool is a 2-way yes/no step (like is a < b?) that yields at most 1 bit of information per step.
- Factorial-scale outcomes: The number of possible final answers grows like $n!$ (or $n^n$)—meaning each of the $n$ items could end up in one of roughly $n$ distinct roles or positions. Not every task on $n$ items has that many outcomes: finding the maximum has only $n$ possible answers and assigning yes/no labels has $2^n$, compared to $n!$ orderings for sorting.
How Existing Algorithms Break $n \log n$
Counterexamples already exist in every algorithms textbook. Two classic ones—Bucket Sort and Radix Sort—sort $n$ numbers in $O(n)$ time when the numbers come from a bounded range or fixed digit width:
- Bucket Sort computes a bucket address directly from each number’s value, drops the item straight into that bucket in a single step (when numbers map cleanly into $n$ slots, that is a direct $n$-way lookup), and then reads the buckets back in order.
- Radix Sort processes numbers one digit at a time. In Most-Significant-Digit (MSD) Radix Sort, 3-digit numbers are first routed into 10 buckets (0–9) by their hundreds digit; only buckets holding more than one item are split again by their tens digit, and so on—without ever comparing two numbers against each other.
Neither algorithm breaks mathematics. Both drop the black-box assumption—and flatten the tree.
Imagine lining up 30 kids by birth month. If you treat them as black boxes and only compare pairs of kids (“who was born earlier?”), you are stuck with a 2-way tree of depth $\log_2 n$. Instead, put 12 labeled boxes on the floor (Jan through Dec). Each kid looks at their own birth month and walks straight to their box in one step.
Computers can do the same thing because numbers aren’t opaque black boxes—they are digits and bit patterns, and hardware can jump directly to a memory address in a single step. Direct indexing widens the branching factor all the way to $n$, collapsing the tree to depth 1. MSD Radix Sort makes the intermediate case just as clear: it routes the exact same items down a tree, except each node has 10 branches (0–9) instead of 2, flattening the depth from $\log_2 n$ down to the number of digits—with zero comparisons. (As we will see next, when numbers are allowed to grow arbitrarily large with $n$, escaping $n \log n$ asymptotically requires choosing the branching factor as a function of $n$ rather than keeping it fixed at 10.)
The Information-Theoretic View
Why does widening the branching factor break $n \log n$, and when is a lower bound truly unavoidable? Information theory puts both assumptions into a single equation.
In an earlier post on entropy, I framed entropy $H$ as the minimum number of binary choices (bits) needed to describe categories of events:
$$ H(\text{outcomes}) = -\sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i $$
That same lens gives us a hard floor for any algorithm.
Let $N$ be the total number of possible final answers to a problem—a function of the input size $n$, not $n$ itself. When every answer is equally likely (the worst case, $p_i = 1/N$), the entropy of the answer space simplifies to:
$$ H(N) = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{1}{N} \log_2 \frac{1}{N} = \log_2 N $$
Why is $H(N) = \log_2 N$ a hard floor for 2-way steps? Let $q$ be the number of 2-way (yes/no) steps an algorithm takes. Those $q$ steps can produce at most $2^q$ distinct transcripts of answers. If $2^q < N$, at least two different final answers must share the exact same transcript, and no algorithm can tell them apart. Therefore:
$$ 2^q \ge N \implies q \ge \log_2 N = H(N) $$
Where does the $\log_2 n$ in $n \log_2 n$ come from? Logarithms turn multiplication into addition:
- When each item has 2 outcomes ($N = 2^n$), taking the log yields $H(2^n) = \log_2(2^n) = n$—linear, with no $\log n$.
- When all $n$ items can be ordered in $N = n!$ ways, you are multiplying $n$ factors that grow with $n$. Taking $H(n!) = \log_2(n!)$ adds up $\log_2 1 + \log_2 2 + \dots + \log_2 n$, which lands at roughly $n \log_2 n$.
Now look at what happens when you widen each step’s branching factor to $k$. Remember from the entropy post that the base of the logarithm corresponds to how many outcomes a single step can distinguish, so $q$ $k$-way steps yield $k^q$ transcripts:
$$ k^q \ge N \implies q \ge \frac{H(N)}{\log_2 k} = \log_k N $$
Notice a crucial distinction here. Any constant $k$-way step only differs from a 2-way step by a constant factor ($1/\log_2 k$): a fixed 10-way decimal lookup trims the work by $\log_2 10 \approx 3.32\times$, and a fixed 256-way byte lookup trims it by $8\times$, yet as $n$ grows without bound (and distinct numbers need at least $\log_k n$ digits), both stay locked to $O(n \log n)$ forever.
To actually escape $n \log n$, $k$ must be a function of $n$ (for example, $k = \sqrt{n}$ or $k = n$). Once $k$ scales with $n$ as $k = n^\alpha$, $\log_2 k = \alpha \log_2 n$ cancels the $\log_2 n$ in $n \log_2 n$, so the total number of steps is only off from a one-shot $n$-way lookup by a constant factor ($1/\alpha$)—that is, linear $O(n)$. Radix Sort achieves this when its base $k$ is chosen relative to the size and range of the numbers (e.g., $k = n$ or $k = \sqrt{n}$): we are using the numerical value of the input itself to inform the algorithm’s addressing, piercing the black box.
Entropy Is a Floor, Not a Guarantee
One important nuance: having $H(N) = \log_2 N$ bits of entropy does not guarantee you can solve a problem in $\log_2 N$ steps (or $\log_k N$ steps with a $k$-way step).
Compare searching a sorted list against finding the maximum of an unsorted list. Both have $N = n$ possible answers, so both have the exact same entropy: $H(n) = \log_2 n$ bits. Yet finding the max takes $n - 1$ comparisons, because each step only knocks out one loser—it cannot cut the remaining candidates in half.
More generally, to reach $q \approx \log_k N = H(N) / \log_2 k$ steps with a $k$-way step over $N$ possible outcomes, each step must partition the remaining candidates symmetrically (evenly) into $k$ disjoint buckets of roughly $N/k$ outcomes. That is what lets every step shrink the answer space by division ($N \to N/k$) and extract the full $\log_2 k$ bits toward the answer.
When a step is asymmetric—say, checking “is item $i$ the target?” on an unsorted list, where one branch isolates $1$ outcome and the other leaves $N - 1$—the worst-case branch shrinks by subtraction ($N \to N - 1$) instead of division, so you never reach $\log_k N$. Finding the maximum runs into a related failure: a > b has two equally likely outcomes, yet on the answer space of $N$ candidate maxima it only discards a single loser, leaving $N - 1$ candidates alive either way because the remaining information is spent on relative order we do not need. You only hit the entropy floor when the problem’s structure lets each step carve the remaining answers into roughly equal, disjoint fractions.
Bringing It All Together
Every complexity claim sits on two axes: how fast the answer space $N$ grows, and how much information a single $k$-way step can extract.
So whenever you see a headline announcing a sub-$n \log n$ algorithm, there are only two ways it happened: either the problem never actually had a factorial-scale answer space in the first place (computing shortest-path distances doesn’t require sorting every vertex, and multiplying two $n$-bit integers only has $2^{2n}$ possible outputs—an entropy floor of $2n$, never $n!$), or the algorithm found a way to look inside the box and widen the branching factor $k$ with $n$.

articles.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of 'Perfect Resilience'
articles.body:
Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
Introduction
One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.
Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.
If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.
Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.
“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira, a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”
Think Globally, Act Locally
Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?
One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.
In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.
This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.
In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.
With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey, a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.
Godfrey, Schapira, and their colleagues showed that in this model, perfect resilience isn’t always achievable. They did so by finding a single example of a network layout that can’t be made perfectly resilient. No matter what set of routing rules you choose, there’s always a pattern of link failures that will cause some packets to get stuck in a loop.
But the network they identified was fairly complicated. Was it a rare example? Or is perfect resilience impossible in many other networks as well?
Minor Problems
The 2012 paper caught the attention of Stefan Schmid, a networking researcher now at the Technical University of Berlin. He toyed with the perfect-resilience problem on and off for years, but his first real progress came in 2020, when he and his colleagues made a connection to a topic in mathematics called the theory of graph minors.
Computer scientists have long studied the mathematical properties of real-world networks by modeling them as graphs — webs of nodes connected by lines called edges. Imagine that you start with a graph, then repeatedly simplify it using three basic operations: You can delete a node, delete an edge, or merge pairs of connected nodes. The graphs that you can obtain by combining these operations are known as the minors of the larger graph.
These operations never make it more likely that packets will get routed in endless loops. If a graph is perfectly resilient, then so are all of its minors.
You can reverse this logic and understand the behavior of large, complex graphs using the properties of their simpler minors. An iconic result in graph theory, called the Robertson-Seymour theorem, tells you what you can learn from this kind of reversal. Applied to network resilience, the theorem states that there’s only a finite number of minors that are not perfectly resilient — every larger graph that lacks perfect resilience reduces to one of these so-called forbidden minors. If you can identify the full set of forbidden minors, you’ll have a complete understanding of when perfect resilience is achievable.
Unfortunately, the Robertson-Seymour theorem doesn’t tell you how many forbidden minors there are, or how to find them. “We know such a finite set exists,” said Matthias Bentert, a theoretical computer scientist at the Technical University of Berlin and Schmid’s collaborator on the new paper. “But we don’t know, does it contain one or two graphs, or does it contain 100,000 graphs?”
The researchers wanted to find the complete set of forbidden minors and prove that no others existed.
In their 2020 paper, Schmid and his colleagues identified two simple graph minors that prevent perfect resilience, but then they got stuck. Schmid suspected they’d need a collaborator with more expertise in graph theory to make further progress. Three years later, he met Bentert at a research retreat, and they worked together briefly on a different problem. In 2025, when Bentert was wrapping up a postdoctoral fellowship in Norway, Schmid invited him to join his group in Berlin.
“It was a really perfect match,” Schmid said. “Matthias made a lot of very fast contributions on a couple of our problems.” Perhaps he’d help make quick work of the perfect-resilience problem, too.
Escaping the Maze
Bentert quickly identified a third forbidden minor. He then decided to see how far he could get by attacking the problem from the other direction. Perhaps if there were no additional forbidden minors — if the three they had found were the complete set — then he could prove that all graphs that lacked these three could be made perfectly resilient.
The strategy worked, but not in the way he had hoped. “I found that, actually, I cannot show it, because it’s not true,” Bentert said. He had discovered a fourth obstruction.
So now they had four forbidden graph structures. Were there more? Bentert tried the same strategy again: Prove that all graphs that lacked these four minors could be made perfectly resilient. The strategy worked, this time because he really had found the full set.
Bentert hadn’t expected the answer to be so simple. “I would have stopped if I reached 50 or so, but that it’s really only four was a little bit of a surprise to me,” he said.
Of course, knowing that perfect resilience is theoretically achievable for any given network is only useful if you know how to choose the right routing rules. Fortunately, Schmid and Bentert’s new result also yields a fast algorithm for finding these rules, which turn out to take a similar form in any network. They’re all based on a trick for escaping mazes: Simply take a right turn at every intersection. The only networks where a maze navigation–based approach fails are those containing one of the four forbidden minors. For those networks, changing the rules won’t help.
Real-World Resilience
With their new result, Schmid and Bentert have fully resolved the perfect-resilience problem as it was originally posed in 2012. But the solution isn’t all good news. Even though there are only four graph structures that obstruct perfect resilience, the fact that they’re so simple means that many networks will have them as minors. Dense networks with many connections are especially likely to lack perfect resilience — an ironic outcome, given that adding more links to a network is the most straightforward way to make it more reliable.
“The more connectivity you have, the more possible subgraphs there are,” Godfrey said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if many real-world networks do not have a solution for perfect resilience.”
That may not be a deal-breaker: In some communication networks, resilience isn’t as critical as high speed and low congestion, two factors that Schmid and Bentert’s rules don’t take into account. And in cases where resilience is important, Schmid and Bentert’s result may not be the end of the story. They now plan to study how the situation changes if each packet can carry a record of the last few nodes it visited. Bentert is optimistic that this approach could make perfect resilience achievable for a broader range of networks, yet still remain feasible in the real world.
“Maybe some very freaky networks will not be perfectly resilient” even in a modified version of the problem, he said. “But everything that will ever be designed by a human or a machine will be.”

articles.title: The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Alma Alexander
Posted on November 25, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi Leave a Comment
Real life mythos and legends often play a role in creating a fantasy world 0f one’s own, and author Alma Alexander has an especially unique myth0logy (one that is personal to her) that she is drawing from for the first book in her new trilogy, The Shadow Before the Dawn.
ALMA ALEXANDER:
Back in the 12th century, a quondam poet wrote an epic that contained the line, “There are only three subject matters for any discerning man: that of France, that of Britain, and that of Great Rome.” Possibly the most immediately familiar one of these would be the Matter of Britain – you will know it as the body of medieval literature associated with Great and with Less Britain (Brittany, for those who recognize it better by that name), and concerned with the legendary kings and heroes associated with it, King Arthur, Lancelot, the Knights of the Round Table, the Holy Grail, all that (mostly, blame Geoffrey of Monmouth). The Matter of France deals with Charlemagne and his paladins, and their wars with Moors and Saracens. The Matter of Rome, or Res Romana, is a more rarefied elixir of Greek and Roman mythology, which includes the Matter of Troy (hence the Odyssey and the Iliad), and which focused on military heroes like Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.
But although those three were “anointed”, as it were, there are very much other “Matters” out there, for various countries and cultures. We might argue about whether Wagner muddied the waters with the Ring of the Nibelungen and twisted Matters of Norse origin and of German origin together in a Gordian knot; the Matter of Spain could be – well – maybe El Cid (Spanish people, feel free to correct me); we might definitely argue about the Matter of America, and about ideas it might contain, such as Manifest Destiny. The Matters of Countries are the invisible backbones upon which the shape of their existence hangs.
There is a Matter hidden deep in Eastern Europe, my own Matter, which talks of a line of Kings who walked into being a line of Saints, who created a kingdom out of a smattering of feeble little fiefdoms, and then forged it into an empire, and then fought a Last Battle in which everything they wrought in the Earthly realm was destroyed but which wrote their lineage into the Heavenly ledgers forever and gave their people the light they needed in order to survive the 500 years of slavery that followed their loss in that Last Battle. I am talking about the Nemanjic Dynasty in the 12th/13th centuries Balkans.
For a long time I have wanted to go back to that ancient tree and pick its fruit. This is my own Matter, the one that belongs to my own background, to my own people. It is a period stuffed with history, mystery, miracles, myths, legends, and larger-than-life characters, ripe for the plucking, and one which is rather less well known to the English-language reading public than the more easily accessible Matters out there. I started on a version of this story years ago, and wrote about 20,000 words of it, and then Life fell on me like a landslide and I lost in quick succession my husband, my mother, and a 19-year-old cat (don’t just dismiss this last; I had raised her from a 9-week-old kitten who weighed less than what it would take to make a decent hamburger when she came into my hands, and her loss HURT).
For six years I was a caregiver and then (in increasingly dense layers) someone who mourned and grieved, and all of that leaves little room for telling stories… so I kind of stopped writing. At all. And then, somehow, I picked up those twenty thousand words and looked at them again. And realized that I needed to tell another story before the story that I set out to tell in the first place. And then I realized that I needed to tell another story before THAT, to give weight and stability to the Matter I was addressing. And just like that, I had a trilogy on my hands.
The Shadow Before the Dawn, book 1 in what became that trilogy, was finally fully formed in 2026. The other books are in process. But that first book… this story matters to me, right from that beginning, deeply, organically. Sometimes I think everything I have ever written was training for this story, these books, to which I feel a true responsibility and which I am dedicated to giving the respect and dignity that they deserve.
Because I am writing a Matter. A story that shaped a nation.
You might not know this story.
Come with me, and let me open the doors into a world full of a magic which may be rich and strange and unfamiliar to you. It isn’t to me. This is my Matter, and it runs in my blood. I hope, when you are done reading this, that you will judge that I have done justice to it.
The Shadow Before the Dawn: Amazon

articles.title: Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds
articles.body:
Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds (apnews.com) 14
			
		 	
				The Associated Press reports:
A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.  But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying.  Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. 
The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.  In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September...
Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in "economic bullying" and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.

articles.title: Anthropic migrated Messages API to Rust with no Rust developers
articles.body:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.
But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.
We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.
In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.
Why migrate?
We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.
This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.
Incremental or all at once?
Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)
The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.
As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.
How we verified the migration
General approaches
To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.
Tests
Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).
The tests were coupled to the Python implementation. An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.
The tests were incomplete. The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.
Detecting parity with production
Production data is sometimes “the only true test” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.
The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.
Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.
Common tools for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies can differ for the same input (Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.
With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.
It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the shape of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:
- Checkpointing. Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).
- Fingerprint. Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.
The result was a shadowing system that produced a small record of each difference between our Rust and Python APIs. Here is an example, with made-up values:
We could then pass this record to an agent to fix it.
Verification loops
Each request that differed left a record in our logs. A single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical diff records. Rather than send each to an agent, we ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by which fields differed, then alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new kind of record. This coordinator assigned a worker agent to own each new kind of record. It also created a new thread in a shared Slack channel where human engineers could follow along and steer it when necessary.
To tackle the many bugs, we set up a series of verification loops. A fast inner loop gave agents a sandbox in which they could test ideas and propose fixes. A slower outer loop then validated fixes in production. In addition, a memory loop recorded any mistakes along the way, saving them so that agents could learn over time (Figure 10).
Inner loop
When we first started testing this in April, we gave each agent a record that showed where the Rust and Python versions differed. Agents would guess the root cause from the code and open a pull request. Once the fix was reviewed and merged, they deployed it to staging, a preproduction copy of the Rust API where we ran the same shadow comparison on test traffic. The agents checked whether the difference was eliminated. Since every hypothesis needed a review and a deployment, feedback was taking hours or days.
We needed agents to get a signal from verification much sooner, so we moved them into their own workspace. We redesigned the inner loop so that agents could have a place to test ideas quickly and fail safely. Each agent ran in a cloud sandbox with both codebases and fast, local checks for what happens before and after the model call. The input check took a request, built the prompt that each version would send to the model, and showed what differed. Because this check never actually called the model, comparing the versions took under a second. We later added an output check, which ran both versions against a fake model. The output check passed a scripted reply, such as a tool call, through each version and compared the results.
The main limitation was that agents could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind each record. So an agent would hypothesize what had caused the difference, then write its own request or model reply to try to reproduce the difference. Since each agent was writing these itself, it could read both results in full. If the results matched, its guess was wrong and the agent tried again. If they differed the same way the record described, the agent edited the Rust until the two versions matched, then added a test that failed on the old code and passed on the new (Figure 11).
The seam between the inner and outer loops was a good checkpoint for human review. Inside the sandbox, a wrong guess cost an agent only a few seconds and had no impact on users. Agents could iterate on their own. We allowed a fix to cross into the outer loop only after it had undergone PR review; this allowed engineers to focus their attention on proposed fixes (rather than on guesses) and on the questions the verifiers couldn’t answer, such as whether a difference between the Rust and Python APIs was the result of a bug or a deliberate change.
Agents posted their fixes and evidence to their Slack threads for engineers to review. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences between the Rust and Python APIs came from web search. The production API retrieved the web search tool’s description from an internal service. The Rust API didn’t call this service yet, so the tool description was missing from the prompts. An agent proposed a shortcut to copy the text into files that would be readable by Rust. The prompts then matched, and the fix passed the local verifier. But an engineer turned it down because it didn’t solve the problem: Rust would still need to call the service before launch, at which point the workaround would be thrown out (Figure 12).
But the verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them. A verifier can tell an agent whether the outputs matched, but not whether the fix is good enough to ship. That’s why human review was an important gate.
Outer loop
In the inner loop, agents debugged differences and proposed fixes. At the seam between the inner loop and the outer loop, engineers reviewed the proposed fixes, gave feedback, and approved them to deploy. The outer loop then compared Rust API deployments with and without each fix.
To make that comparison fair, we logged facts about each request we compared, but not its text, including which model and API features it used—for example, prompt caching, tools, or extended thinking. These details let agents compare requests of the same kind (Figure 13) and ask how often the bug’s fingerprint appeared on builds with and without the fix. This way, agents could monitor the new builds for the bug.
We designed the outer loop to catch problems that the inner loop missed. The inner loop simulated production quickly but imperfectly: agents could test a hypothesis in seconds, but only on requests they had written, and with a local verifier that wasn’t always configured exactly like production.
This means that sometimes a fix passed in the sandbox and production still showed the difference. The agent assigned to the bug would either see the difference in the new build’s records, or be alerted by the coordinating agent. It then went back to the inner loop and used that evidence to form a new hypothesis.
Memory loop
The inner and outer loops fixed one difference at a time. The memory loop improved how agents made those fixes. We didn’t want engineers to have to make the same correction twice, so we recorded what came out of reviews and agents’ own work and applied it to every agent that followed.
For example, when an engineer turned down the web search shortcut (Figure 12), the agent saved a note to memory explaining the decision, the reason for it, and the correct fix, which was to have Rust call the service that supplies tool descriptions.
Building that call took our team weeks, and in the meantime the bug kept producing records. Some had new fingerprints, because the missing text fell at other positions in the prompt or belonged to another tool that used the same service. Agents checked the memory note, recognized the known bug, and linked those records to it, instead of writing another workaround (Figure 14).
Other lessons became general rules for porting and writing Rust. After one agent guessed at Python’s behavior, an engineer made it a rule to port exactly what Python did. An agent then compared the existing code with that rule and found seven more places where the port had relied on a guess.
In June, an agent also went through about 60 of the team’s review comments, grouped the recurring problems and proposed rules, which an engineer edited and approved for CLAUDE.md (Figure 14).
The memory loop also encoded some lessons in permanent checks. This included new tests that failed when Rust drifted from Python, lints that banned patterns reviewers kept flagging, and later a merge check that required anyone changing the Python code to make a matching change in Rust or request an exemption.
Looking ahead
It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.
The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.
Lessons learned
Verification is the new bottleneck. Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.
Verification is how you earn confidence. In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or formal verification can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.
Carefully design the verification signal. A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference in the code and fingerprints helped tell one bug from another.
Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal. Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).
Keep the loops simple, so they scale with Claude’s capability. We tried to put human judgment only into what counted as correct; otherwise we left it up to Claude how to get there. Agents chose which hypotheses to test, how to reproduce each bug, and how to fix it. The verifiers judged the result. Simple loops around strong verifiers allowed us to move productively over time (Figure 16).
Move toward outer loops. At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.

articles.title: Those Five Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa Will Be Detonated Wednesday Morning
articles.body:
Those Five Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals in Iowa Will Be Detonated Wednesday Morning (iowacapitaldispatch.com) 62
			
		 	
				The detonation is back on.  Nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives will be detonated Wednesday morning at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, reports the Iowa Capital Dispatch (part of the nonprofit States Newsroom network 
"The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive."
Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site.   The Army has recommended, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area — a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site — during the detonation period. Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans... 
A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response... Speaking at the press conference Tuesday, Sean Kaufman with HHS said the highest risk is for pregnant individuals, children, or people with chronic illnesses who live or plan to be in the areas the Army forecasts will be impacted.  "You definitely want to be out of that area," Kaufman said of the at-risk groups. "I would evacuate that area that's signaled in the model... "    As many as 100 Iowa National Guard soldiers will be available to aid local, state and federal agencies in their public safety plans [according to a news release from the governor]. They will also help provide guidance and assistance to around 150 households with a temporary evacuation...
At the news conference, acting Secretary of the Army Hon. Adam Telle emphasized that the government's priority was the "health and safety of the citizens of this region."  Telle said those involved have sought advice from "every expert" in and outside of the federal government and have considered all viable options and data before reaching the conclusion to proceed with detonation.
"There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said.  Some of those mitigations include: sand around the structure holding the barrels; two walls of four, 16,000-gallon water tanks; a plan to "flood" the exterior of the storage area with aqueous foam to help absorb particulate matter from the blast; and modeling to forecast impacted areas based on weather conditions.

articles.title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
articles.body:
Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.
EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.
Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.
The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.
Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.
To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

articles.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.
According to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”
But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.
Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.
The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.
404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.
Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.
Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.
The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

articles.title: December 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
articles.body:
December 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Fall $1,800 Innovate Grants for Art + PhotoFeatured
Innovate Grant awards two $1,800 grants each quarter to one visual artist and one photographer. Nine honorable mentions in each category are also featured on the Innovate Grant platform and join a growing creative community of esteemed artists. Applicants must be 18 years and older, and all media and genres are accepted. All applicants retain the right to the work they submit. 
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on December 15, 2026.
Bryson County Retreat Featured
Practicing artists of any background and at any stage of their career are encouraged to apply for a 2027 residency at Bryson County Retreat. Residency periods can be flexible, but month-long stays are suggested. Bryson County is designed to provide ample living and working space and inspirational settings where an artist may work free from the distractions and responsibilities of day-to-day life. The program includes free lodging near tannic dark water lakes, sprawling live oaks, and drooping Spanish moss at the headwaters of the Santa Fe River in north central Florida.
Deadline: Rolling.
Open Calls
Wildlife Photographer of the Year(International)
Alongside its conservation message, this prestigious global competition is hosted by London’s Natural History Museum to champion the work of photographers, whether professional or amateur, young or older, or using top-of-the-range equipment or smartphones. Photographers are eligible for myriad awards, with a Grand Title prize of £15,000. The entry fee is £35 (free for Young WPY contest).
Deadline: 11:30 p.m. GMT on December 3, 2026.
Responsa Foundation Open Call for Textile Art(International)
The Responsa Foundation champions projects that create meaningful social impact and foster public engagement. The organization is seeking textile artists to submit work for This Memory, a group exhibition taking place from September 22 to October 3, 2027, at Burgh House in Hampstead. 
Deadline: December 4, 2026.
Open Call for Public Art Proposals in Moab(Utah, National)
Moab Arts is accepting proposals for 2027 public art projects. Proposals are welcome for sculpture, murals, three crosswalks, and sticker designs but may include other ideas for different media or locations around the city. Preference is given to local and regional artists.
Deadline: 11:59 p.m. MST on December 6, 2026.
Material Works Art Award 2026(International)
Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.
Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.
Call for Mail Art(International)
Hive Center for the Book Arts in Evanston, Illinois, welcomes mail art for the exhibition love|mark, which runs from January 1 to February 27. All submissions must arrive at at the center by December 15 for inclusion in the show.
Deadline: December 15, 2026.
Sony Future Filmmaker Awards(International)
The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards is a major program providing opportunities for creators and filmmakers. The shortlisted filmmakers are flown to Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City, California, to attend an awards ceremony and an industry immersion program. Categories include fiction, nonfiction, animation, immersive, student, and vertical format.
Deadline: 7 a.m. CST on December 15, 2026.
GLEAM 2027 Request for Proposals(International)

articles.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
articles.body:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.
The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.
As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.
Practical EIP takeover
To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.
To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.
Targets
We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.
Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.
Claiming Addresses
By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.
With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:
- Allocate 25 Elastic IPs in the current region.
- Store each address, checking for duplicates.
- Look up each address in the database.
- Keep and log any address that matches a target’s A record.
- Release every address that didn’t match.
- Move to the next region and repeat.
In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.
In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.
The ban hammer
After 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.
Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any issues, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?
We decided not to continue the full attack from the new account to avoid further abuse complaints, and instead decided to reach out to AWS with some suggestions that could make this attack less practical:
- Introduce a new quota on the number of Elastic IPs that can be allocated per month. Using this kind of hard cap rate limit (which could be set to some reasonable amount for large organizations), the attack would be much less likely to succeed.
- Apply abuse restrictions at the organization level instead of at the account level. This would force an attacker to create a whole new organization each time they’re banned, which is more effort.
AWS has since responded. They informed us that they have no plans to change anything here. More on their response in the disclosure section below.
Real takeovers we found
Across our limited target list of bug bounty targets, we were able to claim and control 28 EIPs which matched a live DNS record in the scope, with almost half belonging to government bodies. Bear in mind, we only ran the automation for 48 hours, and we would likely have found more, had we continued.
The most notable were five US Treasury subdomains pointing to addresses we now controlled:
- ftp.treasury.gov
- irssearch.treasury.gov
- pcp.treasury.gov
- rdgw.treasury.gov
- ww5.treasury.gov
We also got hits across a range of public bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, including a university, two government bodies, a financial services company, and a large networking vendor. The rest belonged to Intruder customers, who we reported to directly.
Impact
Once an attacker holds the IP behind a dangling DNS record, they have full control over what that subdomain serves. US government websites tell visitors they can trust a site if its domain ends in .gov and it uses HTTPS - so if an attacker successfully takes over a domain, their site passes the test and users would trust it without question. The attacker can even pass a certificate authority’s domain validation and get a trusted TLS certificate for the domain to make it look completely legitimate.
This legitimacy could lead to phishing using a convincing real government domain to steal users credentials. The attacker could also host services on that domain to gather incoming information, and steal data (e.g. credentials) from any old automations that still point at it. That’s particularly dangerous, since those credentials could provide immediate access to other systems not related to the initial takeover.
A subdomain which has been taken over can also interact with cookies scoped to its parent domain. If treasury.gov sets cookies with Domain=treasury.gov, they are sent to every subdomain, including ones an attacker controls, which could enable session theft in other treasury.gov applications.
How practical is it?
AWS publishes 80 million IPv4 addresses for EC2, and our 450,000 allocated IPs cover 0.56% of that space. At our rate of about 9,400 IP addresses per hour, one account would take a year to cycle through every published address.
That’s slow for an attacker with one account. With multiple accounts, it comes down quickly. If bans really do apply only per account, as our experience suggests, 10 accounts could sweep the full space in around five weeks.
Realistically, the acquirable space is much smaller. Much of it is made up of auto-assigned public IPs or addresses held long-term by other customers, so a real sweep would take less time than these figures suggest.
An opportunistic attacker doesn’t need to cover the whole space to find something worth having. Even at 0.56% coverage, we landed 28 subdomains.
Targeting a specific organization narrows the search. An attacker would start by enumerating the target’s subdomains and identifying records that point to unused EC2 addresses. As AWS publishes the region of each range, they can look up exactly which region to search. For a target in eu-west-2, that’s around 2.2 million addresses rather than 80 million. However, when we allocated repeatedly in the same region, we saw a much higher duplicate rate, slowing the search. A targeted attacker therefore has a smaller haystack, but a slower way of searching it.
Responsible disclosure
All findings were reported through the relevant bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, and affected Intruder customers were contacted directly. We also shared our observations on the abuse controls with AWS.
AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.
Timeline
- Enumerated Elastic IPs - 23rd August
- Submitted findings to bug bounty programs - 25th August
- Reached out to AWS - 8th October
- Received an initial response from AWS - 8th October
- Followed up with AWS - 10th November
- AWS confirmed no plans to fix - 17th November
- Post published - 24th November

articles.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, Stuff
articles.body:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.
Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.
Sponsorship update
It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.
SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.
The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,
possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;
I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.
Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search
because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.
Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?
I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,
how many users I have, or what they’re up to.
At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.
On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,
you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.
I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).
C++ Index…?
Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.
I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.
Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.
Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.
To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.
Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.
I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.
Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.
On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.
“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”
My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.
"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"
Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.
That said, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”—I don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convinced—if AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].
Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.
