articles.title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, Stuff
articles.body:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.
Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.
Sponsorship update
It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.
SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.
The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction,
possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;
I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations.
Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search
because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos.
Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately?
I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from,
how many users I have, or what they’re up to.
At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.
On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,
you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.
I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).
C++ Index…?
Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.
I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.
Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.
Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.
To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be massive, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.
Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.
I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.
Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.
On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.
“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”
My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.
"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"
Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.
That said, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”—I don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convinced—if AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].
Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. articles.title: I've been drinking wine in my kitchen
articles.body:
I’ve been drinking wine in my kitchen
See I don’t even like alcohol much. Like, I’ll have a half-glass of wine at a fancy dinner if everyone else is having some, or one beer at a reception, but that’s it. These days, though, can you blame me?
Yesterday, as you all probably saw, hot on the heels of its proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, Anthropic released a proof of Valiant’s VP≠VNP conjecture—a central algebraic analogue of the P≠NP conjecture, and considered a “warmup” to proving P≠NP since the late 1970s. Then, later the same day, OpenAI released a proof of the VP≠VNP conjecture as well.
You can read all about the VP vs. VNP problem in Section 6.5 of my P vs. NP survey. But briefly, for those tuning in from home, Valiant’s conjecture says that the permanent of an n×n matrix has no algebraic circuits (that is, circuits built out of addition and multiplication gates and constants) of size polynomial in n, unlike the determinant, which does. Anthropic’s result says that a circuit of size exp(Ω(log4/3 n)) is needed, whereas OpenAI gets exp(Ω(log5/4 n)): so, more than polynomial albeit less than exponential. As is often the case, the best known upper bound here is ~2n. The lower bounds are said to work over all fields of characteristic other than 2. (What’s special about 2? Over a field of characteristic 2, addition and subtraction are the same, so the permanent just is the determinant, and is easy to compute!)
From what little I understand so far, the proof techniques in the Anthropic and OpenAI papers look similar. They both do some sort of highly nontrivial “compression” or “shortening,” followed in the end by a diagonalization—the oldest trick in the book! Diagonalization is what should let these arguments evade the infamous natural proofs barrier. There’s probably also a story to tell about how the arguments evade an algebraic-circuit version of the relativization barrier, but I don’t know how to tell it yet.
One immediate implication of these results is that, if you want to map an n×n matrix A to an m×m matrix B whose entries are affine functions of the entries of A, and have the permanent of A be equal to the determinant of B, then m must be exp(Ω(log4/3 n)). This was the question directly targeted by Ketan Mulmuley’s Geometric Complexity Theory program—which, however, these papers don’t use, taking a more direct route to the desired lower bound.
As is de rigueur these days, the proofs come with Lean, formally certifying their correctness to a level considerably beyond what we’d normally demand for a math paper published in a journal. If recent experience is any guide, this will not prevent boatloads of morons from denying that AI could possibly have solved these problems, and latching onto anything whatsoever (e.g., unused Lean code or Lean that deviates slightly from the natural-language version) to declare the proofs to be fallacious … and such claims will then go viral, lapped up by an eager audience on Bluesky and other places hungry for AI denial. If there’s any real technical issue with the proofs, I’ll be happy to hear about it from experts, but my patience for arguing with the flat-earthers is at an end.
Daniel Harlow asked me whether the proof of VP≠VNP raises my confidence in P≠NP itself, which I’d lowered from 97% to 95% in light of OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s recent refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis. I said sure, I’m now back up to 96%.
The possibility that this will be followed up soon by a proof of P≠NP itself has not escaped my notice, or anyone else’s, certainly not at the AI companies. Will the big one come tomorrow? Next week? Next month? In a year? Who the hell knows? Hence the wine drinking, which I wouldn’t call sad, but just … thirsty.
If that wasn’t enough for you—if you still want more—yesterday Sanjeev Khanna, Aaron Putterman, and Junkai Song posted an ECCC preprint with a deterministic linear-time algorithm for finding minimum spanning trees in graphs. (The best previously-known algorithm was ridiculously close to linear time—n α(n) where α is the inverse of the Ackermann function—but not quite. A randomized linear-time algorithm was known.) This was a huge open problem for decades, and one that my wife Dana spent roughly two years working on.
Khanna et al. write, “the main ideas in [our] paper were entirely generated by AI—specifically 6.2 Astra, on a mixture of Ultra and Max effort—with minimal human intellectual intervention. The authors then worked to first carefully verify, and then to simplify and clarify the treatment.”
Anyway, yeah, tonight I’ll again raise my glass, I’ll pray that at the bottom of this terrifying rollercoaster lies a world that my children and I will be glad to inhabit, and I’ll mutter to myself the eternal words:
God would like us to be joyful
Even though our hearts lie panting on the floor;
How much more can we be joyful,
When there’s really something
To be joyful for.
To life, to life, l’chaim!
L’chaim, l’chaim, to life!
It gives you something to think about,
Something to drink about,
Drink l’chaim, to life!
Update: See Lance’s post for more.

articles.title: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
articles.body:
PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.
The text of this post (except the conclusion) was written by Claude. I plan to rewrite it in my own words over Thanksgiving Break but needed to get the project out. So apologies for this move - all of my other posts were written by me, and all future posts will be as well. Even if you find Claude more comprehensible than my meandering thoughts, meander nonetheless I shall.
Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to write cursive. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.
So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.
Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.
How it works
That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.
The data
Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.
The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.
Training a model
I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.
Data and how you show it. Those are the big rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.
The clever parts barely register. Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly worse; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.
Even the transformer is optional, sort of. An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.
Samples
Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.
The drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.
It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.
Picking up a new hand
The trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.
It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.
Reading the letters
One head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.
Do you need captions?
Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?
You can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).
What it can’t do
The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.
Closing thoughts
If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.
I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.
The bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work with it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?
You can’t. The picture-only model has the best likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).
What it can’t do
The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.
Closing thoughts
If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in The Bitter Lesson. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.
I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.
The bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work with it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

articles.title: Here in the World: Letters of Albert Camus, 1944–1959
articles.body:
Joanna Kavenna
Here in the World
Letters: 1944–1959
By Albert Camus & Maria Casarès (Edited by Béatrice Vaillant, translated from French by Sandra Smith & Cory Stockwell)
Penguin Classics 1,175pp £45
Buy this book
What an amazing behemoth of a book! I’ve been lugging it around for weeks. Nearly a thousand letters: the intimate correspondence of Albert Camus and Maria Casarès. When they first met in Paris – on D-Day, 1944 – Camus had already published L’Etranger (1942; The Outsider). Born and raised in Algeria, he was in Paris when the Second World War broke out, and later joined the French Resistance. Camus’s wife, Francine Faure, a mathematician and pianist, remained in Algeria. Maria Casarès was originally from Galicia, the daughter of an exiled former prime minister of Spain, Santiago Casares Quiroga. In 1944, Casarès was already known as an actress, having played the titular role in J M Synge’s Deirdre of the Sorrows. She later starred in Les Enfants du paradis (1945), Cocteau’s Orphée (1950) and La Lectrice (1988), among other films and plays.
On D-Day, Camus was thirty; Casarès was twenty-one. They began an affair, but this ended when Camus was reunited with his wife. In 1945, Faure gave birth to twins: Catherine and Jean. In June 1948, Camus and Casarès met again and embarked on a long relationship, which continued until Camus’s death in a car crash on 4 January 1960. Afterwards, the poet René Char found Casarès’s letters in Camus’s apartment and discreetly returned them to her. In the 1990s, not long before she died, Casarès offered the letters to Camus’s daughter, Catherine.
The correspondence was first published in French in 2017; now it has been (brilliantly) translated by Sandra Smith and Cory Stockwell. The letters are passionate, voluminous, at times torrential. Everything is discussed: love, sex, books, plays, films, beauty, art, family, madness, fear of failure, fear of death. Also logistics, travel plans, inadequate postal services, money troubles, indigestion, hives, headaches.
In her preface, Catherine Camus writes: ‘Their letters make the earth more vast, space more luminous, the air lighter, simply because they existed.’ Casarès, she believes, is ‘like the ocean: breaking, crashing, re-forming and starting over again with stupefying vitality’. Camus is pretty oceanic as well. Both lovers travelled extensively; the letters are often scrawled in haste, sent from Paris, Cabris, Oran, from North and South America, written on ocean liners, or ended abruptly to catch the post. Sometimes, too, they are written as a sort of diary, across several days. The tempo changes. There are lists, schedules; they want to know what the other has been doing, hour by hour. How many glasses of wine they’ve drunk. What they’ve eaten. Who they’ve seen. There are ecstatic protestations of love. And questions, lots of questions. What happened last night? Are you happy? Did you see a doctor? They both emerge vividly – fascinating, erudite, witty, anxious; flawed and paradoxical.
As Catherine Camus says, there is great luminosity; many descriptions of humid summer nights, bright oceans, shimmering mountains. Also, a rich sense of being finite and alive, briefly here in the world: ‘I didn’t sleep any better last night, and tonight it’s so hot, there are so many crickets and stars that I have no hope of falling asleep. At least I can write to you…’ (Camus). Or, ‘Today the sky, which was a drab deep gray this morning, gradually brightened up, and around 2:00, you could just about see the sun peeking through a soft veil’ (Casarès). They struggle with grief, sorrow and anxiety, with physical asperities. Camus endures savage bouts of TB, ‘getting undressed again, letting myself be poked and prodded’. For a while, Francine Faure is depressed, consigned to a hospital, repeating the name ‘Maria Casarès’. Camus and Casarès agonise about her. Sometimes, they argue furiously: ‘You’re stupid, my poor darling!’ writes Casarès, ‘and we must wait for it to pass!’ The war has ended, cities lie in ruins, everything feels untethered and surreal: ‘Of course, the world is still sick, even if I’m well,’ writes Camus. ‘Will we always have to love each other during the Apocalypse, in anguish, in torment?’
Often, they discuss books and authors. They’re not fans of Hemingway. On reading To Have and Have Not (1937), Casarès writes: ‘I certainly found some well-written pages but, my God, how dusty, dull, gloomy it all is, and it smells so much of rooms with peeling wallpaper, all of them a mess, with the odor of sheets, night sweats and dirty clothes!’ Camus’s response is yet more scathing: ‘Hemingway? It serves you right! Why read phonies with no talent?’ Proust gets a mixed review: Casarès is ‘hooked’, loves the way he writes about nature, but finds the ‘political gossip’ boring. In January 1950, Camus sends ‘bad news’:
George Orwell died. You don’t know him. A very talented English writer, who had the same experience as me, more or less (even though he’s ten years older), and exactly the same ideas. He’d been fighting tuberculosis for years. He was one of a very small number of men with whom I shared something.
Both Camus and Orwell opposed the adamantine absolutes of communism and fascism; both were attacked for their political views. They had arranged to see each other in Paris in 1945, but Camus was afflicted by another bout of TB and the meeting never happened. A few months after Orwell’s death, Camus gives a copy of Nineteen Eighty-Four to Casarès. She isn’t convinced: ‘I didn’t learn anything from it that I hadn’t already imagined, and it left a weak impression on me.’
When it comes to his own books, Camus is full of self-doubt, grappling with his ‘tormented, mistrustful soul’. He works ‘like a madman’ on L’Homme revolté (1951; The Rebel), but fears it is a failure: ‘I only hope that this book won’t be too far from what it was meant to be. I hope it will help people to live – that it will say that all is not lost – that it will give everyone with whom I feel solidarity the strength to hate nothing, and to create.’ Even after receiving the Nobel Prize in 1957, Camus is still ‘trying to find some equilibrium within myself’. As for Casarès, in one of the last letters she describes herself as ‘here, a little shapeless, it’s true – a little like you, perhaps, or like the world that surrounds us – but I’m here nonetheless, whole and alive’. It’s impossible to know if they wrote with any sense of eventual publication in mind, or simply and entirely for each other. Camus usually drafted and redrafted his published works. Even his Notebooks were edited – by Camus himself, and by Francine Faure, among others. In the end, these letters are so surreally intimate, so poetic and unbridled, that it feels a bit like reading an extraordinary epistolary novel: about love, art, war, finitude and crazy-beautiful optimism. All is not lost indeed.

articles.title: Defang Security Incident
articles.body:
On November 12, 2026 an attacker copied the credentials we use to run Defang and downloaded a copy of our main database. Here is what happened, what was exposed, what we have done, and what you should do.
On November 12, 2026 an attacker got into the Defang Deploy build system and copied the credentials we use to run Defang. With those they downloaded a copy of our main database. We confirmed this on November 23, 2026. If you have a Defang Portal account, your account is in that database, and this post explains what was taken and what you should do. We are also writing to every affected user by email.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, some of those credentials could also be used against your GitHub repositories and your cloud account. We have replaced them, but there are checks only you can do. They are listed under "What you should do" below. Please go through them as soon as you can.
What happened
We used a separate GitHub App for local development and testing. It was installed on two of our own repositories and had more permissions than it needed, including permission to change deployment environments. Acting as that app, the attacker pushed a commit to one of those repositories and tagged it as a release. Our production environment trusted release tags, so their code ran in our CI with access to our production credentials, and the attacker copied them.
The activity we can see ran from about 06:00 to 10:30 UTC on November 12. The credentials stayed valid until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12. Some of our logs are not detailed enough to rule that out, so we will update this post when we know more.
Timeline
All times are UTC.
- November 12, 06:05: the first workflow that copied build credentials ran, against our development and staging environments.
- November 12, 06:26: our production credentials were copied.
- November 12, 07:57 to 08:10: the database was copied.
- November 15: we were made aware of a security issue with a dependency and installed the update.
- November 23: a routine security scan found suspicious activity in our repositories.
- November 23: we confirmed the database copy from our access logs, replaced our production credentials and emailed every affected user.
- November 24: we published this post.
What the attacker could see
- Your name and email address. This is the address only: the attacker did not get into your email account or see any of your messages.
- Your GitHub or GitLab username, and the names of the organizations that account belongs to
- The answers you gave when you signed up
- If you installed the Defang GitHub App: the names of the repositories it can access, including private ones
- The cloud accounts you connected to Defang (account, project or subscription IDs and regions; no credentials)
- The Compose files you deployed or generated with Defang
- Copies of deployment state from deploys between October 12 and November 19. These can include database passwords and any environment variable built from a defang config value, such as a database URL that contains a password.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: what the attacker could use
The attacker could use the Defang GitHub App's key, and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. The token was stored encrypted, but the encryption key was taken too. Until we replaced them on November 23, anyone holding these could do in your repositories what the app is allowed to do:
- push commits and branches
- change workflow files and start workflow runs
- overwrite Actions secrets and variables
- change deployment environments and their protection rules
- open and merge pull requests
- change repository settings, including branch protection, deploy keys and collaborators
A workflow run started this way can receive your cloud credentials, because the role Defang set up for GitHub deploys trusts workflows in your repository.
If you have billing details with us
The copied credentials included a key for our account at Stripe, our payment provider. Until we replaced it on November 23, someone holding that key could read the record Stripe keeps for you:
- your name and email address
- your billing address, or the parts of it you gave us, and your tax ID if you entered one
- the brand, last four digits and expiry date of your card
- your subscription and invoice history
Your full card number and security code were not exposed. Stripe holds those and does not make them available to Defang or to anyone using our key.
What was not exposed
- Passwords. Defang has none for you: you sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code.
- Your cloud credentials. We never hold them. Your BYOC deployments run in your own account with your own credentials, and Defang's servers have no direct access to that account or to anything running in it. The one indirect path is the GitHub Actions deploy role described above.
- The contents of your repositories. They are not stored in our database.
- Config values you set with defang config. They stay in your cloud account, except for the copies in deployment state described above.
What we have done
- Replaced the Defang GitHub App key and secrets on November 23, and revoked the GitHub sign-in tokens we held.
- Replaced our other production credentials, including database, payment and email credentials, on November 23.
- Signed out every session and invalidated every Defang access token issued before November 23.
- Stopped keeping copies of deployment state on November 19 and deleted the copies we had.
- Cancelled every pending cloud invite link. If you were inviting someone, send a new invite.
- Notified GitHub, who are helping us audit for token misuse.
- Installed the security update on November 15.
- Revoked the development GitHub App's credentials and suspended the app on November 23.
- Reverted the production and staging deployment configurations that were altered by the attacker.
- Notified users and relevant authorities of the data breach.
What you should do
Everyone
- Be careful with email that claims to come from Defang, GitHub or GitLab, especially anything that asks you to sign in, approve an app or share a code. Someone holding this data can write a convincing message that uses your real name and username. We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- You will need to sign in to Defang again.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub
- Check your connected repositories for activity you don't recognize since November 11:
  - new commits, branches or tags
  - changes under .github/workflows
  - workflow runs you didn't start
  - changed Actions secrets or variables
  - new deploy keys or collaborators, and changed branch protection rules
- Look in particular at anything from defang-app[bot]. Your security log is at github.com/settings/security-log; organizations have an audit log under Settings.
- Lock down the deployment environments Defang created. In each connected repository, open Settings, then Environments. For every environment whose name starts with defang-, set "Deployment branches and tags" to your deploy branch only. You can also add required reviewers. This stops a workflow on any other branch from receiving your cloud credentials.
- Revoke and reconnect Defang's access to your GitHub account. In GitHub, go to Settings, then Applications, then Authorized GitHub Apps, and revoke Defang. Sign in to Defang again afterwards.
- If you no longer deploy from GitHub with Defang, uninstall the Defang app from your account or organization.
If you deploy from GitHub Actions: in your cloud account
- Check who has used your deploy role since November 11. The role or identity Defang set up for GitHub deploys has administrator access to your account. A token from a branch or workflow you don't deploy from is a sign of misuse.
  - On AWS this is usually defang-cd-CIRole. Search CloudTrail for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls on it.
  - On Google Cloud, check the workload identity pool's token exchanges.
  - On Azure, check the sign-in logs for the managed identity.
- Narrow that role's trust to the branch or environment you deploy from, if it currently allows any branch.
If you deployed with Defang between October 12 and November 19
- Change your database passwords and any secret that was part of another environment variable, then redeploy. Use defang config set <NAME> for each one.
- If your Compose file has secrets written directly in it, change those too.
If you have billing details with us
You do not need to replace your card. The exposed details are not enough to charge it. Watch your statements as you normally would, and be wary of email or calls that quote your last four digits or billing address to appear legitimate.
If any of these checks turns up something you don't recognize
Rotate the secrets in that repository's Actions secrets and environments and the cloud credentials its workflows can reach, then tell us.
Frequently asked questions
Was my GitHub password exposed? Do I need to change it right away?
No. Defang never had your GitHub password. You sign in with GitHub, GitLab or an emailed code, so there is no password for us to lose.
What the attacker could use was the Defang GitHub App's key and the GitHub sign-in token we keep when you connect GitHub. We replaced the key and revoked those tokens on November 23. Changing your GitHub password is not required, but it does no harm, and turning on two-factor authentication is a good idea in any case. The checks that matter are the ones under "If you installed the Defang GitHub App: in GitHub" above: look for activity you don't recognize, lock down deployment environments, and revoke the Defang GitHub App.
Did they take only my information from GitHub, or did they go further? Did they get my email?
They got your email address, but not your email account. The address we have on file for you is in our database, so it was copied. Defang has no access to your mailbox, so the attacker could not read your email or sign in to your email account through us.
From GitHub, what we hold is your username, the names of the organizations your account belongs to and, if you installed the Defang GitHub App, the names of the repositories it can access. The contents of your repositories are not in our database.
If you installed the Defang GitHub App, the attacker also held the credentials that let them act in your repositories until we replaced them on November 23. We are still checking whether they were used after November 12, and we will update this post when we know more. That is why we ask you to review your repositories and your cloud account. "What the attacker could see" and "What the attacker could use" above list everything.
Did this happen only to me, or to all users?
Anyone with a Defang Portal account is in the database that was copied, so your email address, and potentially your name, was exposed along with everyone else's. Beyond that, what was exposed depends on how you use Defang. See above section for details.
How can I protect my data? How do I check that an email really comes from you?
- Don't sign in, approve an app or share a code because an email asked you to. Open the Defang Portal, GitHub or GitLab yourself by typing the address in your browser, rather than following a link in a message.
- We will never ask you for a password or a token by email.
- Someone holding this data can quote your real name, username or the organizations you belong to. A message that knows those details is not proof that it comes from us.
- If you are unsure about a message, forward it to sec@defang.io and we will tell you whether we sent it.
- Work through the checklist in "What you should do" above. In short: review your repositories, review your cloud account, change database passwords and secrets if you deployed between October 12 and November 19, and turn on two-factor authentication on your GitHub and cloud accounts.
How do I delete my account and data?
Open Settings in the Defang Portal and delete your account there, or email sec@defang.io and we will do it for you.
Contact us
If you find anything suspicious, or want an engineer to go through your account, repositories or cloud account with you, write to sec@defang.io. We will update this post as we learn more.
The Defang Team

articles.title: The Verge’s guide to affordable holiday gifts under $25
articles.body:
Gift-giving on a tight budget is tough, but constraints can also encourage some creative thinking. We thought for a long while (and asked other Verge staffers) about the best items out there, and we’re pretty happy with what we came up with.
The Verge’s guide to affordable holiday gifts under $25
Whether it’s stocking stuffers or a little treat for yourself, these are some of our favorite gifts under $25.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
For this list, we’ve rounded up a barrage of fun gadgets and stocking-stuffer specials. You’ll find nostalgic ways to spruce up a room like Play-Doh’s Blooms, fancy ways to jot down notes like the Pilot Kakuno fountain pen, and plenty of tech-forward extras like the Time Timer Mod. It’s time to get creative with your budget buys, and this list can get you there.
Lamicall magnetic cord organizers
Lamicall’s magnetic cord organizers are simple yet effective tools. They hold the ends of your most frequently used cables so they don’t fall to the floor when you unplug them, and the low-cost accessories can be stuck to the side of your desk or kitchen counter. They also work great behind your entertainment center or wherever else is convenient.
Play-Doh Blooms
There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.
Time Timer Mod (Home Edition)
For visual learners, a visible timeline can help keep the pace moving. The Time Timer Mod provides an aesthetically pleasing 60-minute countdown to help your favorite procrastinator stay on task and maximize efficiency, no matter what they’re working on.
TP-Link Kasa smart plug three-pack
Smart plugs are the easiest way to bring older electronics into the 21st century. For the smart home fan in your life, TP-Link’s Kasa plugs are a brilliant budget-friendly buy, adding Google or Amazon Alexa voice assistance to everyday items, not to mention power schedules and remote control. Note: They support 2.4GHz Wi-Fi connectivity only.
For the giftee who likes to keep things on the level (literally), this striking 12-inch leveling tool offers the traditional bubble measure alongside LED lights that turn from red when the level needs adjusting to green when it locks in. It’s just a slightly more satisfying way to ensure you’re level before drilling or hammering.
Aothia desk mat
Sometimes a little change can make a big difference. Aothia’s desk mats bring aesthetic and functional improvements in an array of stylish color options, with a smooth faux leather surface that protects your desktop and can bring some much-needed order to your desk layout.
These magnetic word tiles are a classic for a reason. Sure, silly phrases or profound thoughts on a fridge door won’t change the world, but they could brighten a housemate’s day. If anything, slowing down a few times a day to read these fun messages as you open the fridge is a welcome break that we all could use.
If you’ve got a scribe on your list who prefers the feel of paper instead of digital screens, give their pencils or fountain pens something to dig into with the Midori MD Note pad. Cream-colored paper, wide lines, and 185-degree binding combine for a great way to jot down anything that comes to mind.
These dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connection, simple setup, and Matter compatibility so they can seamlessly fit into Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home smart home systems. Best of all, these smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.
These Ikea pegboards are a great gift for anyone looking to organize a bedroom, office, or dorm room. They’re available in multiple sizes and colors, and they can be presented in your space in multiple ways, be it mounted on the wall or stood on a desk. Extra accessories make it even easier to organize doodads.
The comedy streaming service created by CollegeHumor alumni offers endless, ad-free entertainment for the improv lover in your life. With multiple shows from some of the top names in comedy, and a business model that encourages profit sharing for creators, it’s a feel-good way to bring more laughter to someone’s life.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.
This moldable material is more than just glue. It’s useful for practical tasks, like fixing drywall, crafting your own cable management system, or just to build for fun. Sugru glue comes in multiple colors and serves as a smart solution to any number of household problems, especially for people who don’t have access to a 3D printer.
Ynesoer automatic soap dispenser
This once-futuristic automatic soap dispenser has become affordable enough for anyone to own. This particular model is one that a Verge staffer owns and likes, thanks to its customizable portions for the perfect hands-free wash. It’s especially great if you cook a lot and don’t want to touch your soap dispenser.
Maxracy garlic roller
For the chef on your list, these convenient garlic peelers make it easy to strip off the skin without crushing the cloves. In other words, it does the most annoying part of dealing with garlic on your behalf. If only it were this easy to tell them they need to take the garlic down a notch in their red sauce.
This truncated version of the popular Wingspan card game offers an easier point of entry in terms of cost and complexity. Players act as bird enthusiasts collecting various types of birds through multiple rounds for their wildlife preserve. Designed for one to five players, each game takes around 30 minutes or less.
These aren’t your grandma’s measuring spoons. Unless, of course, your grandma is super hip and fun, in which case they’re an excellent gift for her, or... she may already have them. With snazzy designs in vivid colors, these silly spoons spice things up in more ways than one.
For those who aspire to use something better than the plain Bic or Paper Mate pen, this affordable fountain pen is great for the aspiring calligrapher on your list. Its design is light and ergonomic, and it includes a single ink cartridge to get them started. This could be the start of a really fun hobby.
Gear Aid Heroclip
Anyone looking for a good stocking stuffer should grab this handy carabiner-style clip. While not everyone will have a use for one, you’ll probably know who on your list will dig its aircraft-grade aluminum frame that supports up to 50 pounds. It even swivels to double as a hanger in a pinch.
Show your support for our journalism while also sprucing up that coffee mug cabinet with a fresh addition. These Verge-branded 15-ounce mugs offer minimalist style and plenty of space for that extra pour you’ll need to make it through the workday, until daycare pickup, or during a long and lazy Sunday.
Sometimes, a straight, regular USB-C cable just won’t suffice. This cable is a fantastic choice for two reasons: First, it’s coiled, letting it expand from around 1 foot to 5 feet; and second, the right-angle connector makes it easier to plug into some difficult-to-reach ports instead of bending.
Get your favorite Pokémon lover a fun piece of merchandise they can piece together. With one of 15 different models (including Slowpoke, our favorite), this model kit includes four different eye sticker options, and at about 4.5 inches long, it fits neatly on a desk, a side table, or on a curio shelf next to other beloved tchotchkes.
Magnetic drawing board for toddler
Finding it hard to shop for that young niece or nephew? We’ve got you covered with this fun and colorful magnetic drawing board, which can be used to focus their creative energy. And maybe, just maybe, it’ll keep them from turning loose on the living room wall with a Sharpie set or crayons.
In the days before Bombas, socks used to be a lame gift. Now, gifting the right pair can make you the hero, especially if you choose pairs like these merino wool socks, which are machine-washable and designed to keep the chill at bay during those cold winter months as well as brisk nights and mornings.

articles.title: Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
articles.body:
Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.
Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.
“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.
In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

articles.title: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
articles.body:
During an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, President Trump said that pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been ensnared in a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy, is “an option,” albeit one that he doesn’t think he will have to exercise.
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president reportedly told the outlet.
Huang, who was ousted from his own company less than two weeks ago, was reinstated Monday. He faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
Huang is scheduled to testify at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week.
When asked about the hearing, Trump reportedly said: “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
At another point in the interview, when asked what he knew about Huang’s other extramarital affairs, Trump reportedly said: “I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex.”
TechCrunch has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: 1Password Security Incident
articles.body:
Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
by 1Password
November 25, 2026 - 4 min
Related Categories
What happened
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.
What information was affected
The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:
- Names and email addresses
- Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
- Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
- Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
- Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
- Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.
When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
What was not affected
- Your vaults and the items in them
- The keys that protect your vaults 
  - 1Password does not store your account password or secret key
- Account recovery keys
- 1Password apps and browser extensions
What we’ve done
- Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
- Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
- Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
- Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
- Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
- Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
- Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
- 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
- Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
- If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

- Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
- Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
- Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
- Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
- Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
- Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
- Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
- 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
- Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
- If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

articles.title: Why Automated Proof-Solving Is the Same Old Dead End
articles.body:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 19 Nov 2026]
Title:The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.
The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

articles.title: Invisible Wave Hits California, Oregon and Canada as Towns Evacuate
articles.body:
On Monday, seawater was already flooding buildings in a small Northern California fishing community, and the worst of this week’s tides had not yet arrived. By Tuesday morning, residents of King Salmon on Humboldt Bay had been ordered to leave. The Humboldt County Sheriff’s Office warned that water levels could climb toward 10 feet if the current tidal anomaly persists, close to the bay’s all-time record of 10.37 feet. Forecasters say sustained southerly winds this week will push the storm surge even higher. Humboldt Bay is only the leading edge of a coastal flood threat that stretches more than 1,000 miles, from Southern California to British Columbia, and it is being driven by a wave almost nobody can see.
That wave is a Kelvin wave, a vast pulse of warm water sent east across the equatorial Pacific by the fast-strengthening El Niño. It does not break on the beach or arrive as a wall of water. It raises the baseline height of the ocean itself, lifting the sea surface along the coast and holding it there for weeks or even months. Forecasters estimate it has raised sea levels off Southern California by 5 to 8 inches, and some projections put the rise at a full foot. On an ordinary day that extra water would barely register, but this week the ocean is starting from a much higher point than usual.
The raised ocean has now arrived at the same time as the king tides, the highest astronomical tides of the year, which happen when the pull of the Moon and Sun line up. This set falls around a full Moon sitting close to perigee, the point in its orbit nearest to Earth, and forecasters say the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle is adding to the push. On top of that, a train of Pacific storms is bringing strong onshore winds, heavy rain and big surf. Each of these things can flood a coastline by itself, and this week all of them are happening together. Forecasters across the region have marked Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day as the most dangerous window.
In San Francisco, the National Weather Service has a coastal flood warning in force through Thursday afternoon, with the highest water expected around 11 a.m. on Wednesday. Forecasters expect the tide to reach about 2.8 feet above normal, almost level with the city’s record of 2.9 feet set during the storms of January 1983. On the Crissy Field gauge, that record reads 8.66 feet, and Wednesday’s official forecast stands at 8.6 feet, less than an inch below it. City officials are preparing for water above 9 feet in case the storm surge comes in stronger than expected.
Mayor Daniel Lurie has called the situation “extremely serious” and urged people to stay off flooded roads and avoid trips that are not essential, though he later said the forecast had improved somewhat. The weather service has flagged extreme flood risk along the bay shoreline, including around San Francisco International Airport and Oakland’s airport. Crews have put up a Tiger Dam barrier system near the Bay Bridge toll plaza, and the state closed the Posey Tube between Alameda and Oakland from Sunday night. On the open coast, breaking waves of 20 to 30 feet are forecast for Wednesday. The Embarcadero waterfront, which flooded in heavy rain only last week, is in the danger zone again.
The bay’s shape spreads the threat well beyond the Golden Gate. Water that enters from the Pacific moves through a large network of bays, sloughs and wetlands, reaching shorelines many miles from the open ocean. Marin County has told residents to take extra care between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. from Tuesday through Thanksgiving. On the Tiburon Peninsula, people in low-lying homes have been urged to think about leaving before each day’s highest tide. Around 1.5 inches of rain is forecast over two days, on top of the 3.2 inches that fell last week, so drains that normally empty into the bay may have nowhere for the water to go.
Southern California has already had a preview. On October 27, king tides arriving with the first push of the Kelvin wave set record high water levels at Santa Barbara, San Pedro, San Diego and La Jolla. In Huntington Beach alone, 114 structures were damaged, and floodwater reached Newport Beach, Long Beach, Redondo Beach and San Diego’s Mission Beach. One Mission Beach resident who had lived there for 30 years said he had never seen flooding like it. Forecasters expect some of those records to fall again this week, less than a month after they were set.
A coastal flood warning covers the whole Orange County coast until Friday, and forecasters say maximum sea levels could top 8 feet from Tuesday through Thursday. Some forecasts suggest Southern California tides could reach 9 feet or more, about a foot higher than October’s record. The weather service office in Oxnard has high confidence in record tides for Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties. Orange and San Diego counties are under extreme coastal flooding and high surf warnings for Thanksgiving Day, with major impacts also possible on Tuesday, Wednesday and Black Friday.
Coastal towns are building defenses as fast as they can. Newport Beach has built or reinforced about 5.3 miles of sand berms, handed out 150,000 sandbags and raised 70 public seawalls. In Huntington Beach, a 3.7-mile stretch of Pacific Coast Highway between Seal Beach Boulevard and Warner Avenue is closed, and low-lying roads are shut from 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. every day this week. Crews in Huntington Harbour are wrapping seawalls in layers of sealed sandbags, and boaters have been told to stay away at high tide because their wakes can push water over the walls. On Dana Point’s Beach Road, ten homes have already been red-tagged and three destroyed, and owners are stacking boulders in front of what is left.
The heat in the water is part of the reason the ocean sits so high. NOAA data from November 12 to 18 showed a wide band of coastal water more than 10°F warmer than the 1971 to 2000 average. Warm seawater expands and takes up more room, which lifts the surface further. Off San Francisco, the sea has also been rising slowly for decades, by about 2 millimeters a year, which means every king tide starts a little higher than the last.
The threat continues north into Oregon and Washington, where weather service offices in Portland and Seattle have warned of coastal flooding through Friday. The worst is expected from Tuesday through Thanksgiving Day, when several weather systems bring strong winds and rising surf during high tide. Forecasters warn that waves could knock people off their feet or sweep them off rocks and into the ocean. Washington State Ferries has already cancelled several sailings because of the high tides, with around 300,000 people expected to use the ferry system over the holiday weekend. Heavy snow in the mountains could also slow travel over the passes, especially on Interstate 90 east of Seattle.
Across the border, Environment Canada says a series of deep low-pressure systems will cross the offshore waters this week, driving storm surge and large waves into the British Columbia coast. Combined with the king tides, these could push water 20 to 50 centimeters (about 8 to 20 inches) above the highest astronomical tide. Water levels are forecast to rise each day and peak on Thursday. Some areas could see 100 to 200 millimeters of rain, the B.C. River Forecast Centre has issued a high streamflow advisory for most of Vancouver Island, and an evacuation alert is in place for some shoreline properties of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation.
Boundary Bay is one of the spots being watched most closely. The bay is wide, shallow and low-lying, and it straddles the border between Delta, British Columbia, and Point Roberts, Washington. The City of Delta has warned that high water could hit Beach Grove, Boundary Bay and Westham Island from Tuesday, with the warning in effect until December 4. The city has put flood protection at beach access points and left sand and sandbags at Seaview Road, the 1A boat launch and the 3rd and 16th Avenue beach accesses.
This week is unlikely to be the end of it. A Kelvin wave can keep the coast raised long after the storms that rode on top of it have passed, and El Niño events usually send five or six of these waves across the Pacific. The 2015 to 2016 super El Niño produced five, and this one is strengthening faster and could become the strongest on record. The next round of king tides is due from December 22 to 26, around Christmas, with more in January, and forecasters say the higher ocean could last into early spring 2027. For towns from San Diego to Vancouver Island, the high water in the coming days may be the first of several rounds this winter.
