articles.title: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
articles.body:
This month’s Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual “Code Red” internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.
Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
In a memo to the teams responsible for Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson revealed the outage was the most significant in history for Microsoft’s customers. “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” said Henderson. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”
As part of this Code Red declaration, Microsoft is focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft now has a target of resolving future outages within an hour, and will reportedly deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose issues. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews.
In a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants.
Microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

articles.title: Smart People Who Give a Shit Use Tools
articles.body:
Anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.
Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.
The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.
I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.
Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.
When you hand a capable model to that engineer, they don’t suddenly shrug and rubber-stamp the first draft. They finally write the TLA+ spec. They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.
The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.
Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve written before about the specific sinking feeling of staring at 800 lines of generated code you have no mental model of and deploying it with crossed fingers.
There’s a subtler hazard too, especially for people early in their careers: if you never wrestle with a weird bug or read a stack trace yourself, you never build the scar tissue that tells you when something smells wrong. And LLMs make laziness unusually tempting because of how they fail. A compiler yells at you loudly when you screw up; a model fails in smooth, confident prose that looks totally reasonable until production catches fire. That’s a genuine risk, and pretending it isn’t would be silly.
Still, look closely at what’s actually broken in that scenario. The trouble comes from shipping code nobody verified, without building a mental model, in an organization where nobody feels on the hook when it breaks. We had that exact engineer long before ChatGPT showed up. Ten years ago they pasted the top Stack Overflow answer without reading the comments, pulled in a bloated dependency to avoid thinking for twenty minutes, and stamped “LGTM” on every review after thirty seconds. Now they can coast as a human clipboard for a model, at least for a while, until the production bugs pile up or someone realizes a cron job could do the clipboard part cheaper. Take away their LLM tomorrow and they won’t suddenly start caring about ACH edge cases. They’ll just go back to shipping carelessness at a slower clip.
Look at Michael’s own example of ACH. The people keeping banking rails alive aren’t chiseling NACHA files into stone tablets to stay spiritually close to the metal. Their care shows up in reconciliation scripts, monitors, static checks, runbooks, and custom tooling they built because unaided human attention breaks down on systems this messy. Every jump up the abstraction ladder (compilers, garbage collectors, search engines, high-level frameworks) brought the exact same warning that we were moving another step away from the machine and losing the people who really understood it. Sure, far fewer programmers today can hand-assemble x86 than in 1985. Meanwhile, the systems we have to keep upright grew by several orders of magnitude. Without stronger leverage, you don’t get a golden age of artisanal engineering where everyone holds the whole codebase in their head. You just get more critical systems that nobody understands at all, because they long ago outgrew what one unaided brain can hold.
There is a bigger elephant in the room about all those outages, too, and it predates LLMs by a long shot. A huge share of the instability we are watching right now is the bill coming due for forty years of insufficient engineering rigor. Giving a shit does not make people infallible. Some of the smartest, most conscientious engineers in the industry spent decades building critical infrastructure in memory-unsafe languages, gluing together under-specified protocols, skipping formal verification, and shipping state machines whose edge cases lived only inside one person’s head. Heroics and tribal knowledge kept the wheels on, right up until they didn’t.
Plenty of the vulnerabilities and failure modes knocking systems over today have been sitting quietly in the wild for years, or even decades. We got away with them because nobody had the time or budget to poke every dark corner of a sprawling legacy stack, and because change moved slowly enough for manual patching to keep up. Only now is the issue being forced, by automated bug-hunting that never sleeps, by decades of accumulated coupling, and by systems that have finally grown too tangled for human heroics to paper over. Blaming all of that on AI slop is a comforting story, because it implies we can just go back to the old way of working and everything will steady out. The old way of working is how we ended up with a world where bad updates and long-dormant bugs can wobble major banks, airlines, and cloud providers in the same week.
None of that lets leadership off the hook. Where Michael is completely on target is what’s happening in the executive suite. Leadership looking at an LLM and thinking, fantastic, now we can lay off the prickly senior engineers who push back on bad ideas and replace them with a $200-a-month subscription, really is a slow-motion train wreck, and it makes a fragile landscape much worse. To someone who has never been paged at three in the morning, a fragile system held aloft by quiet competence and a pile of plausible-looking slop look identical on a quarterly slide deck.
That disease, though, is decades older than generative AI. It’s the exact same management fantasy that gave us “let’s fire the expensive in-house team and outsource the core platform to the lowest bidder,” “let’s cut QA because developers can test their own stuff,” and “let’s lay off twenty percent of engineering while keeping the roadmap unchanged.” AI didn’t invent the belief that engineers are interchangeable output factories. It just handed executives a shinier, cheaper-sounding excuse to run the same playbook again.
That’s why lumping AI-using engineers in with the executives hollowing out their companies does real harm. Telling the story as “AI makes engineers dumb and indifferent” accidentally writes bad leadership an alibi: shucks, the new technology didn’t live up to the hype, who could have known? And on the way there, it sneers at the people in the trenches who are grabbing every piece of leverage they can find to keep increasingly absurd systems from falling over.
If you want to know whether someone gives a shit about a system, asking whether they used an LLM is the wrong question. Ask what happens when the code they merged breaks at two in the morning. Ask whether “the model wrote it” flies as an excuse in code review. Ask whether they have the time, standing, and backing to tell a VP that a deadline is reckless.
Companies lose smart people who give a shit when they strip away ownership, punish dissent, and reward shipping volume over reliability. Give those same people real stakes and a good model, and they don’t check out. They finally get to build the guardrails, proofs, and fixes they never had the hours to build before.
Michael is right that capitalism has its hand squarely on a hot stove right now, and that the rest of us are getting burned while executives relearn that you can’t automate away accountability. I just wish we’d aim the anger at the people making that bet, instead of pretending that giving a shit requires typing every character by hand.

articles.title: Smart People Who Give a Shit Use Tools
articles.body:
Anyone who has worked on payment rails or old distributed systems knows the exact feeling Justin Michael describes in his post this week. You peel back the curtain on some piece of infrastructure the economy quietly runs on, expecting Swiss watchmaking, and find duct tape, twenty-year-old batch files, and three people in the whole company who know why you never reboot box four on a Tuesday. He calls them “smart people who give a shit,” and he’s dead right that they are the main reason the lights stay on.
Halfway down the page, though, the essay takes a turn I’ve been seeing a lot lately, and it bugs me. Michael points to the recent run of big outages (Microsoft 365, United, major banks, Apple) and blames leadership for trying to swap those people out for generative AI. Fair enough; there’s probably plenty of truth in that. But he doesn’t stop at bad management. By the end, the tools themselves have become the acid dissolving whoever picks them up. “Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out,” he writes. Every generated line robs engineers of the struggle that makes them smart and the ownership that makes them care.
The implication is pretty hard to miss: if you’re using AI, you’re giving up on giving a shit.
I use these tools every day on systems where bugs cost significant sums of money or wedge production queues, and my experience has been almost the exact opposite. More than anything else, LLMs amplify who you already are. Deeply curious, caring people can dramatically amplify what they produce and how thoroughly they understand it. Lazy bums can, for now, coast as meat proxies for a chat window, ferrying tickets into a prompt box and clicking merge on whatever falls out.
Think about what “giving a shit” actually meant on a normal engineering team before 2024. Mostly, it meant fighting a losing war against the clock. You’d spot a nasty race condition in a state machine and know you should model it in TLA+, or write a property test that hammers every interleaving, or go read the forty-thousand-line service downstream to be certain your assumption held. Half the time you didn’t, because doing it properly took two days you didn’t have and three other fires were waiting. So you eyeballed the diff, wrote a unit test for the happy path, left a slightly nervous comment, and hoped nobody touched that file for a while. Caring was rarely limited by how much people wanted to do the right thing. It was rationed by how fast one human could read and type.

They pull on the threads they were always curious about, digging into why a gnarly legacy subsystem behaves the way it does instead of treating it as a black box. They build a real simulator for the flaky third-party API nobody ever had time to mock properly. They have the model trace every caller of a legacy function across a sprawling monorepo before changing its contract, instead of grepping for five minutes and praying. They write the exhaustive edge-case tests and run mutation testing against the parts that keep them awake at night.
The kind of rigor that used to be reserved for people writing avionics software or working at Bell Labs is suddenly cheap enough to pull off on an ordinary Thursday. Calling that “caring less” has the whole thing backwards.
Then there is the other side of the amplifier. Anyone who has reviewed a 1,500-line pull request written by a meat proxy who clearly hit “accept all,” got a green linter, and blanked out when asked to explain line 400 knows exactly what Michael is furious about. (I’m certainly guilty of opening massive AI-assisted PRs myself, though in the service of giving a shit, so the line count by itself isn’t the crime.) Prompt, paste, and pray is very real, and it produces miserable software. I’ve written before about the specific sinking feeling of staring at 800 lines of generated code you have no mental model of and deploying it with crossed fingers.

And LLMs make laziness unusually tempting because of how they fail. articles.title: Bypassing iOS Safari's 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
articles.body:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.
More recently, Jordan Walke, creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.
Why the iOS Safari Experience Sucks
What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.
How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.
Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.
High Refresh Rate Interactions
Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.
If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.
In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.
- Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed.
- Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region.
- Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container.
- Want a dial with notches? Snap points!
The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.
Creating “The Controller”
I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.
Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.
First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.
Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. Since it needs a SharedArrayBuffer, we’re forced to use COOP/COEP headers which break cross-origin assets on our website.
What finally worked was using a MessageChannel like before, throttling the next measurement to the next tick using a setTimeout according to the refresh rate of the device, phase-locked to vsync using requestAnimationFrame timestamps. I was nervous about this approach, but as you’ll see later, it panned out well. The only remaining drawback specific to this solution was easy to work around. iOS rounds performance.now() to the millisecond, so I derived the minimum time between draws from the refresh interval.
Each solution got us 80 position reads per second. Two-thirds towards our goal of 120 Hz input.
Safari’s UI process sends the web process one scroll position at a time, and waits for an acknowledgement from the web process before sending another. Anything that arrives in the meantime is overwritten. This was costing us dropped positions. Digging through WebKit yielded what we needed to get around this. It turns out that on every tick where the page has a rendering update queued, Safari flushes the position without waiting. An empty requestAnimationFrame loop is all we need to do that.
This bought us ~12.5% more reads, and brought us to 90 unique position reads per second.
I sort of assumed I had hit the limit of the aforementioned IPC, but it turns out that ProMotion was just deciding that there’s no need to render at a refresh rate higher than 90 Hz.
Squeezing out the last 30 Hz was trickier. A GPU-accelerated CSS animation lets the screen go to 120 Hz, but only while something is scrolling. So a tiny invisible scroller smooth-scrolls in the background, ready to boost us to the full ProMotion refresh rate whenever we need it.
Of course, we don’t want the display pegging to 120 Hz the entire time, so we reserve all the tricks we used to get there for times we expect animations to occur: touch events, scroll-derived animations, etc.
If the interaction you’re building doesn’t need momentum, rubber banding, or snapping, you can forego them entirely and just use a passive touchmove listener on the controller which fires at the full 120 Hz.
Just like that, we’re receiving updates from the controller at a full 120 Hz! Drag the grid below to see.
One issue remains. scrollTop and scrollLeft are rounded to the nearest integer even though iOS scrolls with sub-point precision. Easy fix, thankfully. We just scale the scrollable surface up by the device pixel ratio, then its container back down by its reciprocal.
If you want to use the viewport itself as a controller, you can choose to invasively set the initial-scale in the same way, but this comes with some caveats. You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.
From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.
Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.
Breaking the 60 FPS Render Barrier
Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.
The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?
Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.
Asking Google yields the following preamble.
There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 <canvas> (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.
Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.
Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.
Well, as of today… you can!
At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.
Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.
In WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.
Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.
Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.
Putting it All Together
Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.
Applying Our Learnings
This page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.
When the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.
As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.
On this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.
After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.
Building a Tab Bar Component
Building the Structure
Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.
Layout of Controllers
We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.
Building the State Machine
We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the new events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.
- If a controller is being touched we then magnify & lift the lens.
- We know where to move the lens based on the controller’s offset since the touch began.
- If the user pulls past the bounds of the tab bar, we stretch the bar towards their finger.
- Depending on the offset, when the user stops touching the controller, we settle the lens on the nearest tab.
Adding razzle-dazzle
Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.
Performance
I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.
Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.
Wrapping Up
Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!
Disclaimers
Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

You’ll have to scale units by the DPR, disable text autosizing, and manually scale safe areas. You’ll also get tiny text-selection indicators. All trade-offs, but by no means required.
From here on out, I’ll refer to these scrolling grids as “controllers”, because they act exactly like one. All we have to do is make one invisible and lay it over where we want to read high-frequency input.
Note that the page itself can also be a controller, but Safari will throttle reported scroll positions to 10 Hz during the URL bar resize that happens when you change scroll direction. WebKit skips this if we give the page a scroll-driven animation that animates a non-GPU-accelerated attribute. I went with transitioning between two transparent colours for this page.
Breaking the 60 FPS Render Barrier
Now we get high-frequency input, but the DOM still only updates 60 times a second, so if we tried to leverage it as it stands, we’d just be updating a value twice for every frame that’s drawn. The user would get no benefit.
The vast majority of dragging interactions are already covered by our controllers, and predefined animations are covered by CSS animations. But what about more complicated interactions? What about computation-derived layouts? What about shaders?
Ask your search engine or AI of choice today “How to render canvas content on iOS at 120 Hz without feature flag?” and it will respond that this is a fundamental impossibility in iOS Safari. Even WebKit’s own bug tracker is full of people asking for it. Ink & Switch, game-engine makers. People even cite Capacitor & Tauri as resorting to private APIs.
Asking Google yields the following preamble.
There is no public web API or standard JavaScript workaround to force HTML5 <canvas> (requestAnimationFrame) to run at 120 Hz on iOS Safari without changing the system feature flag.
Fable 5.2 shares the same sentiment.
Short answer: you can't, for JavaScript-drawn canvas frames. On iOS, WebKit caps page rendering updates (which is when canvas content is presented) at 60 Hz unless the user turns off the flag. No web API overrides it. […] Timer-based loops (setTimeout, MessageChannel) won't help, in my understanding: you can draw more often, but the result is still presented at the 60 Hz rendering update. Low Power Mode throttles further.
Well, as of today… you can!
At first, I tunnel-visioned on scroll. I tried breaking workers, pre-rendering permutation “flip-books,” and even live-generating video. It was all too laggy, jagged, or required so much RAM the WebKit process just crashed.
Seven attempts later, and a whole lot of agents digging through WebKit’s source, I landed on this.
In WebKit on iOS, if we create a canvas element and call transferControlToOffscreen, we get an OffscreenCanvas back. The original canvas element becomes a placeholder, and WebKit (following the HTML specification’s recommendation) skips waiting for the next rendering pass when an OffscreenCanvas pushes a frame.
Unlike earlier attempts, without workarounds this is easy on the battery and only uses as much memory as is needed to support a higher-frequency backing store.
Jackpot. We now have 120 FPS rendering on iOS WebKit canvases.
Putting it All Together
Now we can take any input at 120 Hz, and render an output at that very same frame rate. The first thing I created for this was a small UI clone of Ando’s mobile application fitted with a Liquid Glass tab bar, buttons, and buttery smooth navigation interactions. Once installed as a PWA, I kept having to double-take to check I wasn’t in the native application.
Applying Our Learnings
This page is fitted with two custom “Liquid Glass” elements in the viewport. Each of them renders at the full device refresh rate. We have to be very deliberate in order to do this in a way that is performant and convincing.
When the page first loads, we take a snapshot and load it into a WebGL texture. This texture is used as the foundation for a composite that is then fed into our shader.
As the page scrolls, we then sample the region beneath each component, which is all we need to produce our effect. Building it this way means that no matter how the content below it is built, it can decide the best way to keep the texture live.
On this page, components using requestAnimationFrame for illustrative reasons update the texture from the main thread. Components using OffscreenCanvas post their frames directly from their workers to the worker managing the texture. This keeps us off the main thread and lets us get shaders refreshing at 120 Hz.
After all that, the glass just samples a small region around where it would land on the composite texture and computes the frame.
Building a Tab Bar Component
Building the Structure
Let’s build our Liquid Glass tab bar. We’ll start out by just drawing the underlying structure.
Layout of Controllers
We’ll break this down into one controller for each button. Each controller sends us timestamped events: which controller is being used, and how much it has been dragged. We keep a short history of those samples, so we know when a press has moved far enough to count as a drag, and how fast the finger is moving. Nothing else. Everything else is derived from that.
Building the State Machine
We now build a state machine around this. Every frame, the new events go in, and a frame comes out: where the lens is, how far it has lifted and stretched, and how visible the pill is.
- If a controller is being touched we then magnify & lift the lens.
- We know where to move the lens based on the controller’s offset since the touch began.
- If the user pulls past the bounds of the tab bar, we stretch the bar towards their finger.
- Depending on the offset, when the user stops touching the controller, we settle the lens on the nearest tab.
Adding razzle-dazzle
Finally, we apply some shaders to get a convincing Liquid Glass effect.
Performance
I built a benchmark environment and recorded an iPhone 18 Pro at 240 FPS, slowing it down to an eighth to benchmark the difference. The two oscillating squares measure inputs and renders.
Over three seconds of dragging, the controller version averaged 118 FPS while the pointer events version held a steady 60. Even in Low Power Mode, which traditionally limits you to 30, this approach gets you 60.
Wrapping Up
Liquid Glass was the target as an overblown example, but this unlocks a lot. For the first time, you can take input and render output at true device-native speeds on iOS Safari. Micro-interactions feel native and delightful, PWAs which ignored the aforementioned feature flag finally have a way to render at 120 Hz, and look at all the fun we had along the way!
Disclaimers
Would I rebuild my entire application around this? No. Fact remains it’s completely within Apple’s rights and would not violate the HTML specification if they just decided to make OffscreenCanvas’ placeholder wait for the main thread rendering pass. They even have a strong track record of “party pooping” as was done shortly after Lochie Axon unveiled the web-haptics library. I’d much prefer they make these findings moot by disabling the feature flag and natively supporting ProMotion for websites, but Apple is Apple for a reason after all.

articles.title: Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy
articles.body:
Tuesday Jensen Huang Said Nvidia Doesn't Need a Succession Plan, and that He's in Therapy 44
			
		 	
				CNBC reports:
[Jensen Huang] told staff that Nvidia has built a team that doesn't require succession planning the way a normal organization does, because the company operates a unique business model where there are multiple capable leaders at Nvidia that are leading different parts of the organization.  A succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, Huang said, according to one of the people present...
Huang told staff that Tuesday's company meeting was the second hardest meeting of his life, the first one being with his wife. He said he is in therapy, according to one of the people present.   
The Independent notes that Jensen Huang told Nvidia's board Sunday "that he had more affairs beyond the two that were already in the public domain, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter."
Huang was reportedly "contrite" about his behavior during the crunch talks, and the board discussed "the importance of candor and honesty" with him, according to the newspaper.  
Elsewhere CNBC reports even President Trump's "staunchest allies" in the U.S. Congress "recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang..."
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States...."

articles.title: Macrohistory in Six Facts
articles.body:
Joe Stiglitz: “Economists spend enormous energy providing refined testing to their models. Economists often seem to forget that some of the most important theories in physics are either verified or refuted by a single observation, or a limited number of observations (e.g. Einstein’s theory of relativity, or the theory of black holes).”
Can we condense down the most important lessons we’ve learned from macro and macrohistory to a minimal set of facts? Here is one attempt: macrohistory in six (plus or minus) facts.
What I have here on the X-axis is GDP per person, adjusted for inflation and cost of living differences. On the Y-axis is life satisfaction, based on going around and asking people, ‘on a scale of zero to ten, how satisfied are you with your life’.
In richer countries, on average people are happier.
Or – in richer countries, on average people live longer:
Or – in richer countries, fewer babies die:
Are all these good things just coming from people working more? No – in richer countries, people work less; and as countries become richer over time, people work less:
More intangible things, too. You can ask people how much they trust their neighbors. In richer countries, people trust their neighbors more:
Of course, we know market capitalism has its flaws – for example, richer countries emit more CO2 per person:
And all of this is correlation not causation.
But we’re going to run with this, and use GDP per person as our measure of how well we are doing.
Which brings us to:
This is the most important fact about human history.
We are ∼10 times richer than our great-great-great grandparents, who themselves in turn were ∼2 times as rich as Jesus of Nazareth.
Everyone used to be poor. This is the most important fact about macro history.
Why did we used to be poor? We lived in a Malthusian hellscape:
This shows the real wage of workers in England since 1250.
Prior to the Industrial Revolution, any time wages rose, more babies would survive to adulthood, parents would have more babies, and the population would rise until wages were driven back to subsistence.
We lived in a Malthusian hellscape. Until:
The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in human history.
We went from 0.01% growth per year, up to 0.1% with the Industrial Revolution around 1750, to 1% with the Second Industrial Revolution around 1870, to the modern 2% growth rate.
The Industrial Revolution was the single most important event in macro history. It also brought about:
The growth explosion from the Industrial Revolution did not take place everywhere and all at once. Many countries did not see faster growth and rising GDP per person until much later – and many still have not seen these much at all.
But let’s talk first about the frontier.
This is the most important fact in modern macro. Growth at the technological frontier – measured here as GDP per person in the United States – has been a shockingly steady 2% per year for the last 150 years.
You can see a temporary blip down for the Great Depression, but otherwise the trend has been remarkably constant.
Running water, electricity, automobiles, computers, the web – all show up here as a continuation of a steady 2% per year trend.
What about the rest of the world?
The figure here has on the X-axis, income per person per day. You can see, for example, that even the poorest 11% of people in the United States have on average a higher income than the median person in Bangladesh or Ethiopia.
Income varies enormously across countries. Those of us born in the United States are so, so lucky.
Well, are we stuck with these enormous differences? No:
Here again we see the United States up top as the frontier.
Japan and South Korea, at the turn of the 20th century, were ∼as poor as sub-Saharan Africa is today. But Japan and South Korea caught up close to the United States. There are growth miracles.
But there are also growth disasters. Argentina at the turn of the 20th century was one of the richest countries in the world. But it has stagnated, relative to the frontier. A classic basket case.
And there are countries like Nigeria, which have never experienced much sustained growth at all.
What should we expect of the future? This takes us to the most fun fact, the most speculative:
Over the long sweep of history, aggregate GDP growth is speeding up.
What I have plotted here is how long it takes for world GDP to double. This goes back to 1 million years ago. Measuring GDP in 1 million BC is hard, but for our purposes I feel good about these numbers.
We’ve gone from doubling every 100,000 years down to a modern doubling time of every 35 or so years.
———
Now, to the natural question: what should we expect about growth in the future?
I think it really comes down to: which prior do you want to anchor to?
Do you want to anchor to the last 150 years or so, with our constant 2% growth and doubling every 35 years?
Or do you want to anchor to the long sweep of macrohistory, where growth has been speeding up?
We live in a weird time.
Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff?
This is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.
I found these “Six Big Facts of Macrohistory” particularly useful as framing when teaching my undergrad macro course for the first time last fall: teaching GDP construction (fact 0), the Malthusian model (fact 1), the theories of the Industrial Revolution (fact 2), the Solow model (facts 3-5), and the endogenous growth model (fact 6).
It was pedagogically very useful to have this catechism of the Six Facts to review at the start of many classes, to anchor the students to where we were in the course.
It was also useful for me, for setting a target for the bare minimum that students might remember in a decade. Do I expect them to remember the capital accumulation equation of the Solow model? No. Or even the idea of income vs. substitution effects? For the vast majority – no, not really.
Can I hope that they pick up a gut-level sense, in their bones, that everyone used to be poor? That’s an extremely important idea, a realistic goal, and yet an idea that the vast majority of people do not know or have not properly internalized.
I also think the Six Big Facts of Macrohistory is a useful attempt to condense “what should any well-informed civilian know about macro and macrohistory”. E.g. my microeconomist wife, or my parents.
What are the runner-up facts not listed here? Structural transformation and urbanization? The demographic transition? Women’s emancipation or rising health would be the natural top candidates, but are captured (if perhaps buried) in Fact 0.
Again, underlying these figures is the astounding work of generations of economic historians, demographers, national statistical agencies, and others.

articles.title: Nfs2root: A 12-year-old pre-auth remote root in the Linux kernel's NFS server
articles.body:
Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in. We pointed OpenSec's Antara at it. It came back with a root shell.
Pre-auth heap overflow in the Linux NFS server (nfsd)
Fixed in Linux 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1. Update the kernel and reboot.
What you need to know
- What: a pre-auth heap overflow in the kernel's NFS server, nfsd.
- Who: any Linux host serving NFSv4.1 or 4.2 (the default) on a reachable tcp/2049.
- Impact: one TCP connection writes 61 bytes past a kernel heap object; chained, that gives a root shell.
- Now: patch and reboot. Until then, firewall tcp/2049.
Key facts
- Severity 9.8 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N)
- Attack Remote, unauthenticated, tcp/2049
- Impact Kernel heap overflow → remote root shell
- Bug age 12 years, since Linux 3.16 (2014)
- Affected In-kernel nfsd with NFSv4.1 or 4.2
- Fixed in 6.12.117 · 6.18.61 · 7.3.2 · 7.4-rc1
One connection, no login
The NFS server runs inside the kernel and parses network input before it knows who you are. CVE-2026-99362 lives in that gap: a client can shrink its reply cache to zero bytes, then make the server copy a full reply into it. The copy lands on the kernel heap, and the client picks most of the bytes.
Twelve years in a few lines of C
Timeline
- Commit 47ee52986472 narrows the reply buffer while handling SEQUENCE. It ships in Linux 3.16.
- 12 yearsEvery kernel since 3.16 carries it: LTS, distribution and appliance kernels.
- Jérémy Jean of ANSSI sends a fix upstream with a KASAN report.
- OpenSec's Antara flags the bug, scores it 9.8 and turns it into a root shell on its own.
- CVE-2026-99362 is published with fixes.
Watch it run
A real run, end to end. Left: the victim's console. Right: our client on another machine, talking to the victim only over tcp/2049.
Root cause
Each NFSv4.1 session slot caches its last reply, so a retried request is answered exactly once. The client decides how big that cache is.
Set it to the minimum and every slot's buffer is zero bytes. nfsd4_sequence() then shrinks the reply buffer to that limit before it accepts the slot. Pad the request's tag so the buffer fills right after the SEQUENCE opcode, and the encoder quits without flagging an error. The server believes SEQUENCE succeeded and caches the whole reply, headers and tag included, into a buffer with room for nothing.
That is 80 bytes copied, 61 of them past the end of the heap object, 40 of them chosen by the client.
The fix checks that the reply fits before taking the slot, and makes the encoder report what it can't fit.
From overflow to root
The exploit stays private. Each step is an ordinary NFS request:
- Overflow The write corrupts the neighbouring slot's bookkeeping.
- Leak A replay request returns 3.8 KB of kernel heap, and with it the KASLR slide.
- Free A forged pointer makes the kernel free an object we choose.
- Reclaim We refill that memory with a fake callback built from NFS client names.
- Trigger We hang up. nfsd calls the fake callback, and the kernel runs /bin/sh as root.
In the recording, that command is whoami; id; poweroff -f: the victim prints root, then uid=0(root), and switches itself off.
Found and proven by a machine
Antara, OpenSec's white-box harness, flagged the nfsd reply-cache path, scored it 9.8, and built the leak, the arbitrary free and the root shell shown in the video by itself: end to end, with no human in the loop.
Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host.
Am I exposed?
Tick what's true for your host. All four means exposed, today.
Am I exposed?
What to do
Patch and reboot
On a distribution kernel, install the update that lists CVE-2026-99362.
Can't patch today? Close 2049
Or turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2
Then restart nfs-server. This turns off pNFS and some 4.2 features.
Hunting for it
The attack is valid NFS, so there is no network signature. Look for:
- Kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, on every attempt, successful or not.
- Oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames.
- Shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server.
- Bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source.
Disclosure
We reported the bug to the NFSD maintainers and security@kernel.org on 22 September 2026 with the full remote-root exploit, and sent a patch the same day. CVE-2026-99362 was published with fixes on 20 November.
Credits
- OpenSec Intelligence: found the bug with Antara, which escalated it to pre-auth root on its own, and reported it with the full exploit and a patch.
- Jérémy Jean (ANSSI): found it independently and wrote the upstream fix, 5d5a72e965c8 and 241848cc774e.
- Chuck Lever and Jeff Layton: the NFSD maintainers.
References
nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slotThe upstream fix for CVE-2026-99362, by Jérémy Jean.github.com nfsd: set op->status when an operation's header cannot be encodedThe follow-up guard in the NFSv4 encoder.github.com
- Introduced by 47ee52986472 (Linux 3.16)
- Patch thread
- OpenSec's patch submission

articles.title: The year the web industry gave up
articles.body:
The year the web industry gave up
I’ve been drafting my personal “year in review” and one topic stood out as needing its own follow-up. So let’s get that out of the way!
Twenty twenty six, what an uneventful year, eh?
That’s sarcasm. The entire year has been nothing but incessant chatbot addicts toking their token pipes and shouting: “Everything has changed! Don’t get left behind!”
Despite regularly being mistaken for a software “engineer” I am but a humble website developer. And by “website developer” I mean website developer, not React developer; very different. Not that anyone understands this anymore. I’ll be lambasted for making fallacious “no true Scotsman” arguments for asserting that real web dev has actual standards.
Nevertheless, today I’m talking about/to the real web industry.
What’s left of it, anyway.
The web industry
TL;DR: the web industry is dismantling itself from the inside.
Events of the last year have been incomprehensibly stupid. The rapid deskilling and decimation of professional talent is a shock to the system. It’s demoralising to see once-respected peers drop all pretence of care for their profession.
Every week I sigh “et tu, Brute?” as I strike off another peer from my Christmas card list.
Web professionals are cashing in their credibility to shill for the AI industrial complex. People who have spent years, decades in some cases, building a reputation as leaders within the web industry are now destroying what they’ve built. They step on the heads of those who are fighting to stay afloat. I don’t need to name names, they won’t shut up about their chatbots. You know the type. They gush AI platitudes as if the singularity is holding a gun to their head. And they’ve solved everything! Web development? Chatbot. Web design? Chatbot. The websites they’re building? Believe it or not; chatbots.
And what has the web industry actually gained after all this performative slop?
- Entry level jobs have evaporated
- Web development education is in the gutter
- Web infrastructure is getting hammered
It’s embarrassing how much the web industry has lost in so little time. It has cannibalised itself and those responsible seem oblivious to the cause and effect of their actions.
Let’s get one thing absolutely clear: there is no career in prompting. There is no scenario where replacing your work with a chatbot will have a long-term positive impact on your career. Unless you’re into S&M at the beck and call of billionaires. I mean, I don’t want to kink shame, but keep it out off the workplace, please!
The “it’s just a tool” and “inevitable” rhetoric doesn’t cut it. For heaven’s sake, even if you continue to ignore all other moral an ethical issues, at least open your eyes to the absurdity of what’s being sold here. Tokens are not the commodity, you are.
Replacing professionally trained skills with markdown files and ceding control to chatbot subscriptions is not a sustainable future for the web industry. What’s left of it, anyway.

articles.title: Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You'll Be the Main Character.
articles.body:
Google Wants To Make a 24/7 AI TV Channel. You'll Be the Main Character. (404media.co) 58
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader schwit1 shares a report from 404 Media: Google has filed for a patent that would use the information it knows about you to create an AI-generated TV channel full of personalized "shows" starring you and featuring customized advertisements. The patent is the latest signal of the AI video endgame: endless highly specific, customized content that is automatically generated based on the wealth of data companies and advertisers collect about you.
Tech companies regularly file for patents that they don't end up actually putting into real products, but this one, called "creating a channel of video experiences tailored to a user," describes a system that many AI companies have been clearly trying to build. It imagines something called "My Channel," which would be filled with AI content generated based on demographic data, their video watch history (presumably from YouTube), and other information it knows about the user. It would then make "the user as the protagonist for the whole video." The patent was first noticed by Patentlyze, a news site that tracks tech company patents, who shared it with 404 Media.
"You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist," a hypothetical LLM prompt in the patent reads. "The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the  of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the  of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The  and  parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred."

articles.title: 40 Deliciously Easy Make-Ahead Breakfasts for Christmas Morning
articles.body:
We independently select these products—if you buy from one of our links, we may earn a commission. All prices were accurate at the time of publishing.
X
Loading Email Sign-Up Form...
Depending on how you celebrate, Christmas morning might mean presents to open, church services to attend, or family to visit. Whatever it means for you, making a big-batch breakfast ahead of time comes in clutch (especially if you’re planning on cooking a special dinner later in the day).
Whether you prefer sweet or savory (or both!), we’ve rounded up some of our absolute favorite Christmas morning breakfasts. And the best part is, they all can be made in advance. These 40 make-ahead breakfast recipes include the best homemade cinnamon rolls, cheesy breakfast casseroles, and more. And because they give you a little time back to enjoy Christmas morning, they’re one of the best gifts you can give yourself.
Credit: Photo: Alex Lepe; Food Styling: Brett Regot
Layered with scrambled eggs, ham, cheese, and Dijon, these croissant breakfast sandwiches can be made in advance so you can spend more time with the family on Christmas morning.
Make these hearty breakfast burritos stuffed with fluffy scrambled eggs, crispy hash browns, pork sausage, and a special spicy creamy sauce in advance. Simply heat them up for a quick and delicious Christmas morning breakfast.
Don't be fooled — this breakfast casserole feels fancy but is so easy to make and perfect for whenever you have guests over. It's got serious croque madame vibes.
This moist and tender loaf is even better than the one from Starbucks. Plus, it starts with a full can of pumpkin, so you don't need to worry about having any left over.
This strata is essentially a savory bread pudding with eggs, sausage, and cheddar cheese, and is perfect to make the day before. Simply bake it on Christmas morning.
These cranberry scones are flaky, not too sweet, and bursting with pops of brilliant cranberry in every bite. The rum glaze makes them special-occasion-worthy.
Cinnamon buns make all mornings better. These have a little roasted sweet potato purée in the mix, which gives the dough a beautiful burnished-orange color, just the right amount of moisture, and a hint of earthy sweetness.
As long as you have a few vegetables and some eggs on hand, you can have this frittata on the table in minutes. Even better, make it the night before and heat it up in the morning.
This breakfast casserole is a delicious way to add more veggies to all the heavy food on Christmas day. Spinach, peppers, potatoes, and mushrooms all make an appearance!

articles.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
articles.body:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann
Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the
axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.
- grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md.
- grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.
Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.
Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).
The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.
Apache 2.0, Copyright 2026 Anthropic, PBC. See LICENSE, and NOTICE and
ATTRIBUTION.md in each folder.

articles.title: Britain's ghost stations
articles.body:
When I stepped off a train at Achanalt station into the frosty Highlands one morning last March, I did notice that it wasn’t quite Waterloo in the rush hour, but I didn’t realise what an exclusive club I had just joined. According to a list of Britain’s most and least-used stations published this week, I was one of only 352 people to board or get off a train there in the entire 12 months from April 2025 to March 2026.
Flanders and Swann wrote ‘The Slow Train’ about the Beeching closures, lamenting the rural stations which were to close. They needn’t have worried: over half a century on, such places still exist.
My instinct is to attack the waste of public money in keeping a station open when hardly anyone uses it, but the absurdity of Britain’s ‘ghost’ stations fascinates me more than angers me. In any case, having paid £11 to travel 20 miles down the line from Strathcarron, I did rather feel that I had single-handedly covered the annual cost of maintaining what is really little more than a platform and Perspex shelter.
Achanalt, it turns out, is only the 15th least-used station in Britain. The honour of being the least-used this year is taken by Reddish South, on an obscure line from Stockport to Stalybridge in Greater Manchester, which was used by only 94 passengers. It is an achievement it will be hard-pressed to repeat next year, as the country’s least-used station invariably receives a leap in custom as railway fanatics descend on it just for the sake of being there: station-visiting has apparently taken over from train-spotting now that few trains have proper locomotives any more. Last year’s winner of the title for least-used station, Elton and Orston, in Nottinghamshire, saw its annual passenger numbers jump from 68 to 102, demoting it to third place. I wouldn’t be surprised if every single one of the extra passengers wore an anorak and carried a bag of Marmite sandwiches.
There are two types of ghost station. Firstly, there are those such as Reddish South which are the product of public opposition to the Beeching closures. Some time in the 1970s, British Rail stopped closing stations, reckoning that the bureaucracy and expense of going through the consultation procedure required to remove them from the railway map altogether was greater than simply running down the service to a minimal level. As a result, Reddish South receives one train a week in each direction, on a Saturday morning. You can’t even get a day out in Stockport: catch the 8.46 from Reddish South and you only get five minutes before the train home.
The second type of ghost station is those like Achanalt, which offer a full service of several trains a day; it is just that there aren’t many people who want to travel there. In Achanalt’s case, it isn’t hard to wonder why. The ‘village’, if it can be called that, consists of four houses. Nor is the station all that much good for doing what I was doing: accessing the nearby hills, as a river cuts them off to the south and a thick forestry plantation lies in the way to the north. If you want to go for a walk, it is almost certainly going to involve a few miles’ romp along the A832.
It is pretty absurd that Dr Beeching left a station like this open while depriving Dudley (population 335,000) and Mansfield (114,000) of a rail service – although the latter has subsequently reopened. But at least Achanalt serves four properties. Even more bizarre is Altnabreac station on the Far North Line between Inverness and Wick.
Maybe Dr Beeching couldn’t even find it on the map. It lies up a track seven miles from the nearest public road and there is precisely one house within five miles: the former station house. Trouble is, owners, who presumably could have bought a remote property anywhere in the empty vastness of Caithness, don’t seem to like trains very much. In 2023, a gang of workers from Network Rail turned up to repair the platform and found the gate locked. After a stand-off lasting many months, involving many lawyers and a court case, and a threat by Network Rail to compulsorily purchase the property so that access could be restored, an injunction finally gave the work gang access.
In the meantime, no trains ran at all: the official passenger numbers for the year 2024/25 were zero. Happily, services have now been restored and the walkers and bird-spotters have returned to the platform. Er, all 172 of them last year.

articles.title: Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release
articles.body:
Anthropic, OpenAI Employees Fear Models Are Too Unsafe to Ever Release (axios.com) 22
			
		 	
				Axios reports:
Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates...
The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen, sources told Axios. 
Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely... Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.  This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. 
There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

articles.title: Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe
articles.body:
Amazon Drone Crashes On Garage After Delivering Shampoo, Draws FAA Probe (arstechnica.com) 112
			
		 	
				The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has opened an investigation into an Amazon Prime Air delivery drone that struck a fiber-optic cable and crashed onto a residential garage in Michigan after delivering shampoo. The drone lost a propeller and became entangled in power lines, prompting Amazon and local utility workers to coordinate its removal. Amazon offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card. Ars Technica reports:  Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case -- so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as "UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff." That notice was posted on November 23. The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents. 
Amazon said the Michigan crash was the first involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit, but federal regulators are already investigating several incidents in Arizona and Texas involving collisions with a construction crane, an internet cable, and an apartment building.
An Amazon spokesperson said Prime Air drones make nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered "hundreds of thousands of packages this year."

articles.title: Deriving Black-Scholes
articles.body:
Deriving Black-Scholes
Option price from the no-arbitrage hypothesis.
Even if it feels unintuitive, the price of an option does not depend on whether you expect the underlying to moon or tank. Under some reasonable market hypotheses, we can build a fully hedged portfolio by holding the underlying and shorting the option. Since it is riskless, by no-arbitrage assumption, it must return the same as the risk-free interest rate. That allows to put together an equation (the Black-Scholes equation), and solve for the option price (the Black-Scholes formula).
Model §
A European call gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying at a fixed price \(K\!\), the strike, on a fixed date \(T\!\), the maturity. Its value \(V\!\) is the premium you need to pay for having that optionality, and it depends on time and on the underlying stock price \(S\!\). At maturity it is the payoff1 1 For example, pay $5 today for the right to buy one AMZN share for $200 in a month. If AMZN then trades at $230, you buy at $200 and the option is worth $30. If it trades at $180, you walk away and the option is worth nothing.
\[V(T,S)=\max(S-K,0).\]
Stock moves scale with price, so it is common to model the returns instead of the price. Over a short time the return is a small drift plus noise. The noise is the sum of many small, unpredictable2 2 Weak-form efficient market hypothesis: past prices do not predict future moves. sources. Such sum can be modeled as a Brownian motion \(W\!\),3 3 By the central limit theorem, the sum of many small independent variables is normal. so the return is
\[\frac{dS}{S}=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW\!,\]
with drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma\!\). For our model, we will assume constant drift, volatility and interest rate \(r\!\). We will also assume “perfect” trading, with fractional shares allowed, no fees, no taxes, no dividends, and no arbitrage.
Hedged portfolio §
The trick of Black-Scholes is to build a fully hedged portfolio combining the option and the underlying in the right proportion. By the no-arbitrage hypothesis, its returns must be the same as the interest rate \(r\!\), and that way we can put together an equation.
When the stock moves a little, the option moves by \(\Delta\) times as much, with
\[\Delta=\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}.\]
If you short one option and hold \(\Delta\) shares, then the two moves cancel. This is a delta hedge.
Note that \(\Delta\) changes with the stock price and time. The portfolio is riskless only over an instant, and stays so only if it is rebalanced continuously.
Black-Scholes equation §
Use the Taylor expansion of the option value and keep the terms up to order \(dt\). Since \((dW)^2=dt\), the \((dS)^2\) term is one of them,
\[dV=\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}dt+\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}dS +\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}(dS)^2.\]
Substituting the stock model gives
\[dV=\left(\mu S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt +\sigma S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\,dW.\]
Now, we can use the same hedged portfolio \(\Pi\) as before, short one option and long \(\Delta\) shares, which is worth \(-V+\Delta S\!\). Holding \(\Delta\) fixed over an instant,
\[d\Pi=-dV+\Delta dS,\]
and substituting \(dS\) and \(dV\!\) gives
\[d\Pi=\left(-\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} -\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt.\]
See how noise and drift cancel. No \(dW\!\) term is left, and everything else is known at time \(t\), so over the next instant the portfolio change is fixed.4 4 A known return with no randomness is precisely what riskless means. We’ve built a riskless portfolio, that by the no-arbitrage assumption, it must earn the risk-free rate, \(d\Pi=r\Pi\,dt.\) Equating both expressions gives us the Black-Scholes equation
\[\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}+rS\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}=rV.\]
Note that \(\mu\) is gone, so the option price does not depend on the drift.
Black-Scholes formula §
I won’t bore you with the technical details,5 5 For the details, see John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 11th edition, Pearson, 2021. The Bible of derivatives. but the above equation can be solved by a change of variables to turn it into the heat equation, whose solution is known. Define
\[\tau=T-t,\quad x=\ln S+\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau,\quad V(t,S)=e^{-r\tau}w(\tau,x),\]
where \(w\) is the option value at maturity. Substituting, all terms but two cancel, and we get the heat equation
\[\frac{\partial w}{\partial\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial x^2}.\]
With the payoff as initial condition, the solution is
\[w(\tau,x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2\tau}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \max(e^y-K,0)\,\exp\left(-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2\tau}\right)dy.\]
Completing the squares gives the Black-Scholes formula
\[V(t,S)=S\,N(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2),\]
where \(N\) is the standard normal CDF and
\[d_1=\frac{\ln(S/K)+\left(r+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{\tau}.\]
- \(N(d_1)\) is the hedge ratio \(\Delta\), so the first term represents the price of an asset-or-nothing call, which pays the share if the call ends in the money.
- \(N(d_2)\) is the risk-neutral probability of exercise, so the second term is the present value of the expected strike payment.
That’s all, lads, go make Ken Griffin broke.

articles.title: Swift Death of Statelessness
articles.body:
Swift Death of Statelessness
My drive home from work is always spent in total silence. The monotony of Route 101 (it's not a flex) has an uncanny way of clearing cognitive noise. Today, somewhere in that quiet stretch of highway, reflecting on my work in the Kubernetes ecosystem, it struck me just how completely our industry is reinventing itself.
For 15 years, cloud computing was worshiping a statelessness as an absolute deity. Build stateless containers, spin them up dynamically, let them die without consequence. And this architecture was simple, resilient, and economically predictable.
And then AI happened, violently dismantling prior art. Reasoning models and multi-turn agentic workflows are inherently stateful. Every interaction carries a prompt history, a context window, and an expensive KV-cache. When you route a prompt to an arbitrary node using standard round-robin load balancing, you discard that cache. You force saturated GPUs to recompute tokens that were already processed milliseconds ago.
In economics, we call this pure deadweight loss. In distributed systems, it's referred as cache thrashing. The architectural frontier of networking is no longer about blindly moving packets from point A to point B. It is an economic allocation problem: balancing network transport latency against the marginal cost of GPU recomputation.
We spent a decade decoupling state from compute. Now the laws of physics and economics are forcing us to design intelligent proxies to put them back in the same room.
